stem: Patient presented to the ER with pelvic fracture, he is actively bleeding with a large hematoma in the pelvis, his BP = 80/50 (or something near to this), most appropriate management?
key_concept:
Unstable pelvic fracture: resuscitate, bind, then control the bleeding vessel.
  • Hemorrhagic shock: blood products early (balanced transfusion)
  • Pelvic binder to reduce pelvic volume
  • FAST to look for an abdominal source
  • FAST positive: laparotomy; FAST negative: angioembolization or preperitoneal packing
  • Most pelvic bleeding is venous or from fracture surfaces; arterial bleeding suits angioembolization
exam_pearl: A pelvic hematoma alone is not an indication for laparotomy; a positive FAST is.

stem: 72 year old female underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Post operatively she complains of fever, tachycardia and leukocytosis. In examination of the wound there was slight erythema and no pus formation. Temperature: 38.6, HR: 116, BP: 90/60. Which of the following is most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: slight erythema and no pus formation
why_right: She meets several SIRS criteria at once: temperature "38.6" (above 38), "HR 116" (above 90) and "leukocytosis". The wound shows only "slight erythema and no pus", so no infective source is confirmed, which makes SIRS the best label rather than an infection diagnosis. SIRS is the body's systemic response to the surgical insult itself and is common early after an operation. The "BP 90/60" is not a SIRS criterion; it signals possible evolving sepsis, but sepsis still needs an identified or suspected infective source.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thrombophilia is a predisposition to clotting, not a cause of fever with leukocytosis; it would matter only if she presented with DVT or PE.
B. UTI is a classic cause of fever around postoperative days 2 to 3, but nothing here points to it (no urinary symptoms, no catheter or urinalysis findings).
C. Surgical site infection needs real wound signs such as purulent discharge, spreading cellulitis or a collection, typically around days 4 to 5; slight erythema without pus does not establish it.
key_concept:
SIRS = 2 or more criteria; sepsis = SIRS plus a confirmed or suspected infection.
  • Temperature above 38 or below 36
  • HR above 90
  • RR above 20 or PaCO2 below 32 mmHg
  • WBC above 12,000, below 4,000 or more than 10% bands
  • Severe sepsis = sepsis plus organ dysfunction; septic shock = refractory hypotension
  • Postop fever: D1 atelectasis; D2 to 3 UTI, pneumonia, thrombophlebitis; D4 to 5 wound infection, DVT
exam_pearl: Criteria met but no proven source = SIRS; add a pus-draining wound or positive urine and it becomes sepsis.

stem: A patient presents after total thyroidectomy with numbness around the mouth and in the peripheral limbs. What is the most likely cause?
OptD: Hypocalcemia due to vitamin D deficiency
why_right: "Numbness around the mouth and in the peripheral limbs" after "total thyroidectomy" is the classic picture of hypocalcaemia. The cause is hypoparathyroidism from injury, devascularisation or inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands, usually appearing within 24 to 72 hours. Look for Chvostek and Trousseau signs and check serum calcium.
why_wrong_block:
B. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness, aspiration or stridor (if bilateral), not perioral and limb paresthesia.
C. Postoperative hypothyroidism develops over weeks as stored hormone runs out and gives fatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain, not acute tingling.
D. It does produce hypocalcaemia, but vitamin D deficiency is a chronic background cause; symptoms starting right after total thyroidectomy point to parathyroid damage.
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy complications by presentation:
  • Neck swelling with stridor within hours: hematoma, open the wound at the bedside
  • Hoarseness or aspiration: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high-pitched voice: superior laryngeal nerve
  • Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm: hypoparathyroidism, so hypocalcaemia
  • Refractory hypocalcaemia: check magnesium
exam_pearl: Tingling after thyroidectomy = parathyroids, not nerves; voice change = nerves.

stem: 14 year old pt with ulcerative colitis failed to respond to many medical therapies. Patient has fulminant disease complicated by toxic megacolon, which of the following is the most appropriate URGENT treatment?
highlight_terms_source: fulminant disease complicated by toxic megacolon
why_right: UC that has "failed to respond to many medical therapies" and is now "fulminant" with "toxic megacolon" carries a high risk of perforation, so the URGENT definitive treatment is surgery. The emergency operation is a subtotal/total colectomy with end ileostomy, done after rapid resuscitation (IV fluids, nil by mouth, IV antibiotics and steroids). These supportive measures stabilise the patient for surgery but do not replace it once medical therapy has failed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Methotrexate is a slow-acting maintenance immunomodulator with no role in acute severe colitis or toxic megacolon.
C. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics are part of supportive care for toxic megacolon, but they treat translocation and sepsis risk, not the failing colon; alone they are not the urgent treatment after failed medical therapy.
D. TPN or bowel rest is supportive nutrition only and does nothing for the toxic dilated colon; it would only be the answer for nutritional support questions.
key_concept:
Toxic megacolon in UC: resuscitate, then decide surgery early.
  • Toxic megacolon: colon dilated above 6 cm plus systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis)
  • Initial: IV fluids, NPO, bowel decompression, IV steroids, IV antibiotics
  • Failed medical therapy, perforation or worsening: urgent colectomy
  • Emergency operation: subtotal/total colectomy with end ileostomy
  • Ileal pouch reconstruction is a later elective stage, never in the emergency
exam_pearl: If the stem says medical therapy has already failed, the answer is colectomy, not more drugs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: '14 y old boy with ulcerative colitis have toxic megacolon. Urgent management? A - IV fluid and avoid oral intake, B - colectomy, C - Antibiotics, D - Methotrexate' (unmarked).

stem: A 68-year-old man has been advised to undergo surgical treatment for a left reducible inguinal hernia. He is otherwise healthy. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
why_right: An "otherwise healthy" man with a primary, unilateral, "reducible inguinal hernia" who has been advised surgery gets a tension-free open mesh repair (Lichtenstein). Mesh lowers recurrence compared with suture repair, and the open approach is the standard default for a first unilateral hernia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Simple (suture or tissue) repair without mesh has a higher recurrence rate; it is reserved for situations where mesh is avoided, such as a contaminated field.
C. Laparoscopic repair is preferred for bilateral or recurrent hernias, when faster recovery is a priority, or for femoral hernia; none applies here.
D. Non-surgical management (watchful waiting) suits minimally symptomatic patients or those unfit for surgery; this patient is healthy and already advised to have surgery.
key_concept:
Choosing the inguinal hernia repair:
  • Primary unilateral, healthy adult: open mesh (Lichtenstein)
  • Bilateral: laparoscopic
  • Recurrent after open repair: laparoscopic (operate through fresh planes)
  • Need for faster return to work: laparoscopic
  • Strangulated or contaminated: emergency open repair, mesh often avoided
exam_pearl: Bilateral or recurrent flips the answer to laparoscopic; a single primary hernia stays open mesh.

stem: Patient did thyroidectomy he developed a peri oral tingling so diagnosis?
key_concept:
Match the post-thyroidectomy symptom to its cause:
  • Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm: hypoparathyroidism, check calcium
  • Fever, tachycardia, agitation: thyroid storm
  • Hoarseness: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high pitch: superior laryngeal nerve
  • Neck swelling with stridor: hematoma
exam_pearl: Paresthesia = calcium problem; hyperthermia and tachycardia = thyroid storm.

stem: Patient hypertensive, tachycardic, no obvious external injury. What is the type of shock?
key_concept:
Read HR and skin to type the shock.
  • Hypovolemic: HR up, cold peripheries, SVR up
  • Neurogenic: HR normal or low, warm peripheries, SVR down, neuro deficit
  • Septic: HR up, warm early, infection source
  • Cardiogenic: HR up, cold, raised PCWP
  • Obstructive: tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive PE
exam_pearl: Tachycardia rules toward hemorrhage; bradycardia with warm skin after trauma is the neurogenic clue.

stem: Hypotensive tachycardic GCS low
key_concept:
ATLS order: treat what kills first.
  • A: airway with cervical spine protection; intubate if GCS 8 or less
  • B: breathing, decompress tension pneumothorax
  • C: circulation, stop bleeding, IV fluids or blood
  • D: disability, GCS and pupils
  • E: exposure with temperature control
  • Secondary (head-to-toe) survey and imaging only after stabilisation
exam_pearl: Fluids are part of C; when asked for the first step, the whole ABCDE primary survey beats any single intervention.

stem: 25 year-old MVA patient. Suffering head trauma in the process. He is conscious but disoriented
why_right: Any "MVA" trauma patient starts with the primary survey (ABCDE) to find and treat immediate life threats, even when "conscious". Being "disoriented" after "head trauma" is assessed under D (GCS, pupils), but airway, breathing and circulation must be secured first. Imaging and detailed examination come only after the primary survey and resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Head CT is indicated (GCS below 15 after head injury), but only once the primary survey is complete and the patient is stable enough for the scanner.
C. Head-to-toe examination is the secondary survey, done after the primary survey and resuscitation, not first.
D. Observation is unsafe in a disoriented patient after a road traffic accident; it suits a fully alert patient with minor head injury and no CT criteria.
key_concept:
Trauma sequence: primary survey, resuscitation, secondary survey, definitive care.
  • Primary: Airway with C-spine, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure
  • Disability: GCS and pupils identify head injury severity
  • GCS 8 or less: secure a definitive airway
  • Secondary survey: head-to-toe exam and history
  • Imaging such as head CT follows stabilisation
exam_pearl: Head CT is tempting with confusion after head injury, but nothing comes before ABCDE.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' follow-up printed under 1234; lead-in question not recalled.

stem: 55-year-old woman presents with a scaly, oozing lesion on the right nipple for the past few weeks. On physical examination, no palpable breast masses are found. Breast ultrasound and mammogram are normal. What is the next best step in management?
highlight_terms_source: scaly, oozing lesion on the right nipple
why_right: A "scaly, oozing lesion" of the nipple persisting for weeks in a "55-year-old" is Paget disease of the nipple until proven otherwise. Normal mammogram and ultrasound do not exclude it, since it may be confined to the nipple or associated with occult DCIS. The diagnosis is confirmed by a nipple (punch, wedge or full-thickness) biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Referring to dermatology delays tissue diagnosis of a possible malignancy; eczema that is bilateral, itchy and spares the nipple or responds to treatment may suit dermatology, a unilateral nipple lesion does not.
B. A topical steroid trial can falsely improve Paget disease and delay diagnosis; it is reasonable only for typical bilateral areolar eczema, with biopsy if it fails.
key_concept:
Paget disease of the nipple vs eczema:
  • Paget: unilateral, starts on the nipple then spreads to areola, older woman
  • Eczema: often bilateral, itchy, starts on the areola, spares the nipple
  • Normal imaging does not exclude Paget
  • Diagnosis: nipple biopsy
  • Most cases have underlying DCIS or invasive cancer
exam_pearl: Persistent unilateral nipple eczema in an older woman = biopsy, not steroids.

stem: A 45-year-old obese woman presented with 1-week history of jaundice, anorexia and abdominal pain. She has no chronic illnesses and not on any medications. On examination, she is jaundiced with stable vital signs and no fever. Abdomen exam showed mild tender liver with span of 13 cm, no splenomegaly. Labs: RBC 4 (4.2-5.4 female), Hb 110 g/L (120-160 female), platelets 212, WBC 18 (4.5-10.5), direct bilirubin 79 (1.5-6.5), total bilirubin 98 (3.5-16.5), AST 70 (12-40), ALT 150 (5-40), alkaline phosphatase 1000 (39-117). Which of the following is the next step in the management?
OptD: Abdominal CT scan of the liver
why_right: A raised "direct bilirubin 79" with a markedly raised "alkaline phosphatase 1000" and only modest transaminase rise is a cholestatic pattern. The first step is abdominal ultrasound to check whether the bile ducts are dilated, separating extrahepatic obstruction (such as stones in an "obese" 45-year-old woman) from intrahepatic cholestasis. It is cheap, noninvasive and widely available.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRCP is second-line imaging, used when ultrasound is equivocal or to define the level and cause of an obstruction before intervention.
B. Liver biopsy is invasive and only considered for intrahepatic cholestasis after imaging excludes duct obstruction.
D. CT is less sensitive than ultrasound for gallstones and adds radiation and contrast; it suits suspected malignancy or staging after ultrasound.
key_concept:
Approach to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia:
  • High AST and ALT: hepatocellular injury
  • High ALP and GGT: cholestasis, then ultrasound
  • Dilated ducts: obstruction (stones, tumor, PSC), then MRCP or ERCP
  • Normal ducts: intrahepatic causes (PBC, drugs, sepsis, pregnancy)
exam_pearl: Cholestatic labs always mean ultrasound first; MRCP and ERCP come after.

stem: A 20-30s male patient presented to the ER complaining of a perianal painful lump for 12 hours, which he felt after the passage of a hard stool. On exam, there is a 1 x 1 cm dome-shaped, bluish, tender swelling just beneath the perianal skin. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall is keyed to lateral sphincterotomy, reasoning that the lump followed straining with a "hard stool", which links it to anal sphincter spasm as in fissure disease. Note that the actual findings (a "painful lump" for "12 hours", "1 x 1 cm dome-shaped, bluish, tender" swelling "just beneath the perianal skin") describe a perianal hematoma (thrombosed external hemorrhoid). Sphincterotomy is the standard operation for a chronic anal fissure; see the concern note before relying on this key.
why_wrong_block:
A. Conservative care (analgesia, stool softeners, sitz baths) is the standard approach for a perianal hematoma that presents late (beyond about 72 hours) or with mild pain; this recall's key instead targets the sphincter.
B. Rubber band ligation is for internal hemorrhoids above the dentate line (grade I to III); it must never be applied to an external, sensate lump below the dentate line, which is what this is.
D. Aspiration does not empty a thrombosed external hemorrhoid because the content is clotted blood; early evacuation is done by incision or excision, not needle aspiration.
key_concept:
Painful bluish perianal lump after straining = perianal hematoma (thrombosed external hemorrhoid).
  • Early (within about 72 h), severe pain: incision/excision and evacuation of the clot under local anesthesia
  • Late or mild: conservative (analgesia, sitz baths, stool softeners)
  • Same lump + fever + raised WBC = perianal abscess: incision and drainage
  • Chronic fissure (>6 weeks): lateral internal sphincterotomy
  • Acute fissure (<6 weeks): topical diltiazem plus constipation treatment
  • Rubber band ligation: internal hemorrhoids only
exam_pearl: A LUMP points to hematoma or abscess; sharp pain on defecation with NO lump points to fissure, the only one where sphincterotomy applies.

stem: Old age male with lesion on right thigh. Lesion was well demarcated, red, painful to touch. What's the next investigation?
highlight_terms_source: well demarcated, red, painful to touch
why_right: A "well demarcated, red, painful to touch" lesion on the thigh of an older man is an inflammatory or infective skin picture (erysipelas or cellulitis), not a pigmented tumour. The question asks for the "next investigation", and ultrasound is the quick bedside test that shows whether there is an underlying abscess (which would need drainage) and helps exclude a deeper collection. It is cheap, fast and radiation free.
why_wrong_block:
A. Punch biopsy is for a suspicious skin lesion needing histology (an atypical rash or a possible tumour); an acute tender red area is an infection picture, not a reason for biopsy.
B. MRI is reserved for suspected deep infection such as necrotizing fasciitis (only if it does not delay surgery), osteomyelitis or a soft tissue mass; it is not the first test for a superficial red lesion.
C. X-ray helps only if gas in soft tissues, a foreign body or bone involvement is suspected; it cannot show a soft tissue fluid collection.
key_concept:
Red, tender, demarcated skin lesion = soft tissue infection; image to look for pus.
  • Erysipelas: sharply demarcated, raised, tender, fever; group A strep; penicillin
  • Cellulitis: ill-defined redness after minor trauma
  • Suspected abscess: ultrasound, then drain any collection
  • Necrotizing infection: surgery first, imaging must not delay it
  • Pigmented irregular lesion: excisional biopsy, not ultrasound
exam_pearl: Red and painful = infection, so ultrasound for pus; dark and irregular = melanoma, so excisional biopsy.

stem: Female came to the ER after MVA with severe abdominal pain, BP 83/50 (no Hb level was mentioned). What is the initial step?
why_right: After an "MVA" with "severe abdominal pain" and "BP 83/50", this patient is in hemorrhagic shock from presumed intra-abdominal bleeding. Current trauma resuscitation (ATLS) favours early blood products over large volumes of crystalloid in a hypotensive trauma patient, so packed RBC transfusion is the initial step while the bleeding source is identified. A normal Hb at this point would not be reassuring, because Hb lags behind acute blood loss.
why_wrong_block:
A. Crystalloid may be started as a limited bolus, but "observe" is unsafe in a hypotensive trauma patient; large crystalloid volumes dilute clotting factors and worsen bleeding.
B. Laparotomy is the definitive step for an unstable patient with a positive FAST or peritonitis, but resuscitation with blood starts first and runs alongside the decision to operate.
key_concept:
Hypotensive blunt abdominal trauma: resuscitate with blood, then FAST decides.
  • Stable: CT abdomen
  • Unstable blunt: FAST
  • Unstable + FAST positive: laparotomy
  • Unstable + FAST negative: DPL / look for another source
  • Unstable stab wound: laparotomy
  • Hemorrhagic shock: early blood products, limit crystalloid
exam_pearl: Do not wait for an Hb result in a hypotensive trauma patient; Hb lags behind acute bleeding.

stem: Young female presented to ER with severe shoulder pain, with visible deformity of the shoulder, inability to abduct the arm. What is the next step in evaluation?
why_right: "Severe shoulder pain", a "visible deformity" and "inability to abduct the arm" suggest a shoulder dislocation (most often anterior) or a proximal humerus fracture. Plain X-ray (AP plus a lateral or axillary view) is the first investigation: it confirms the dislocation and its direction and shows any associated fracture before reduction is attempted.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI is for soft tissue injury such as a rotator cuff or labral tear, usually after reduction or for persistent symptoms; it is not the first test for an acute deformity.
B. CT is used for complex fractures (for example of the glenoid or humeral head) when X-ray is inconclusive or for surgical planning, not as the first step.
D. Surgical exploration is for hard signs of vascular injury (pulseless limb, expanding hematoma); nothing here suggests a vascular injury, and a dislocation is reduced closed after X-ray.
key_concept:
Suspected dislocation or fracture: X-ray first, then reduce.
  • Anterior dislocation (most common): arm held abducted and externally rotated, squared-off shoulder
  • Posterior dislocation: seizure or electric shock, arm adducted and internally rotated
  • Check axillary nerve (sensation over the deltoid) before and after reduction
  • Post-reduction X-ray to confirm position
  • MRI later for rotator cuff or labral tears
exam_pearl: Always X-ray before reducing a shoulder: a hidden fracture changes the plan.

stem: Patient underwent sigmoidectomy using previously used surgical instruments. Which measure now helps reduce the risk of surgical site infection? (it was written what will reduce in this scenario)
why_right: The scenario's problem is that "previously used surgical instruments" were used, so the measure that removes this source of contamination is proper sterilization of instruments before the next operation. The question is general rather than about this patient: nothing done now reverses the exposure, but correct instrument sterilization is what prevents surgical site infection going forward.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotic prophylaxis works when given before incision (within about an hour); continuing antibiotics after surgery does not lower SSI rates and promotes resistance, so it is not recommended.
B. Keeping the patient warm during surgery is a genuine SSI-reducing measure in general, but it does not address this scenario's specific failure, which is contaminated instruments.
D. Unsterile instruments clearly raise infection risk, so saying there is no effect on the wound is false.
key_concept:
SSI prevention bundle (match the measure to the failure in the stem).
  • Sterile instruments and aseptic technique
  • Prophylactic antibiotic before incision, not prolonged afterwards
  • Hair removal by clipping, not shaving
  • Normothermia and glucose control
  • Skin antisepsis (chlorhexidine-alcohol)
exam_pearl: Prophylactic antibiotics count only BEFORE the incision; postoperative antibiotics are a classic wrong answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: The Q is general, not about this patient.

stem: 56 year old male, past history of peptic ulcer, present to ER with severe abdominal pain, tenderness all abdomen, guarding, Rebound, Skin cool and clammy, Hypotensive 87/60, Heart rate 120, Initial management?
why_right: A "past history of peptic ulcer" with generalized tenderness, "guarding, Rebound" points to a perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis. The patient is in shock ("Skin cool and clammy", BP "87/60", HR "120") from fluid loss into the peritoneum, so the initial step is IV fluid resuscitation. Laparotomy is the definitive treatment, but it follows resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Laparotomy (omental patch for a duodenal ulcer) is the definitive treatment of a perforated ulcer, but it comes after fluid resuscitation; operating on a hypovolemic patient is dangerous.
C. Vasopressors are only for shock that persists after adequate fluid; giving them to a volume-depleted patient worsens organ perfusion.
key_concept:
Perforated peptic ulcer: resuscitate, confirm, operate.
  • Clinical picture: sudden severe pain, rigidity, rebound, absent bowel sounds
  • Initial: IV fluids, NPO, NG tube, IV PPI, IV antibiotics
  • Imaging: erect chest X-ray for free air under the diaphragm
  • Duodenal perforation: omental (Graham) patch
  • Gastric perforation: biopsy the edge (exclude cancer) and patch or excise; gastrectomy only for large or malignant ulcers
exam_pearl: "Initial" management in any shocked surgical abdomen is fluid; "definitive" is surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: A follow-up 'Q:' version (BP 85/55, options IV fluid / vasopressor / blood transfusion / antibiotic) is carded separately; it also highlights IV fluid.

stem: Known case of peptic ulcer presented with abdominal pain tenderness and rebound tenderness with guarding blood pressure was 85/55 and tachycardia 120 what the initial management?
why_right: A "known case of peptic ulcer" with tenderness, "rebound tenderness with guarding" means a perforated ulcer with peritonitis, and "85/55" with "tachycardia 120" means shock. The "initial management" is IV fluid (crystalloid) to restore circulating volume; antibiotics, imaging and surgery follow once resuscitation is under way.
why_wrong_block:
B. Vasopressors are added only when hypotension persists despite adequate fluid; in a volume-depleted patient they worsen tissue perfusion.
C. Blood transfusion is for hemorrhagic shock (for example a bleeding ulcer with melena or hematemesis and a low Hb); here the picture is perforation with peritonitis, not bleeding.
D. IV antibiotics are part of managing perforation and peritonitis, but restoring circulation comes first in a hypotensive patient.
key_concept:
Peptic ulcer complications: the picture decides the first move.
  • Perforation + shock: IV fluid first, then antibiotics, PPI, laparotomy
  • Bleeding ulcer + shock: fluid resuscitation, transfuse if Hb low, then endoscopy
  • Vasopressors: only after adequate volume
  • Erect chest X-ray: free air confirms perforation
exam_pearl: Peritonitis signs point to perforation (fluid, then surgery); melena or hematemesis points to bleeding (fluid or blood, then endoscopy).
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 1281 (numbered version had options IV fluid / laparotomy / vasopressor).

stem: After minor Injury painful swelling in forearm with warmth Next step?
key_concept:
Warm painful swelling after minor injury: decide by fluctuance and toxicity.
  • Diffuse, no fluctuance: cellulitis, antibiotics (IV if systemic or severe)
  • Fluctuant or collection on ultrasound: abscess, incision and drainage
  • Pain out of proportion, toxicity, purple skin: necrotizing fasciitis, urgent surgery + IV antibiotics
  • Firm enlarging mass, not inflamed: imaging + biopsy, then wide excision if sarcoma
exam_pearl: Fluctuance is the switch: no pus means antibiotics, pus means drainage.

stem: A 5-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a rapidly progressive painful skin lesion. The pain is severe and disproportionate to the physical findings. Over a short period, the lesion has increased in size with progressive swelling and discoloration. On examination, the child is febrile and appears toxic, and the affected area shows erythema with patches of purple discoloration and marked tenderness. What to do?
OptB: surgical consultation and iv antibiotic (exactly like this)
highlight_terms_source: pain is severe and disproportionate to the physical findings
why_right: "Rapidly progressive" painful lesion, pain "disproportionate to the physical findings", a "toxic" febrile child and "patches of purple discoloration" describe necrotizing fasciitis. It is a surgical emergency: urgent surgical consultation for debridement plus broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, because the infection spreads along fascia faster than the skin shows.
why_wrong_block:
A. MRI can show fascial involvement, but waiting for imaging delays debridement and raises mortality; the diagnosis is clinical and confirmed in theatre. Imaging is only for unclear cases in a stable patient.
C. Topical antibiotics and analgesia suit only minor superficial infections such as impetigo; they have no role in a deep, life-threatening, toxic soft tissue infection.
key_concept:
Pain out of proportion + rapid spread + toxicity + skin discoloration = necrotizing fasciitis.
  • Treatment: urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics
  • Usually polymicrobial; group A strep can cause it alone
  • Crepitus and foul smell suggest gas-forming organisms
  • Perineal and genital form: Fournier gangrene
  • Cellulitis: localized redness and pain, no toxicity, antibiotics alone
exam_pearl: Pain out of proportion to what you see is the flag that turns "cellulitis" into a surgical emergency.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 1317 (numbered 1317 is a different forearm swelling recall).

stem: Patient presented with symptoms of appendicitis. Imaging: appendicitis, fecolith, appendicular abscess 1 x 15 cm reaching the flank. What is the management?
why_right: Imaging shows appendicitis with a fecolith and an established "appendicular abscess" (large, "reaching the flank"). An organized appendiceal abscess is treated by image-guided percutaneous drainage with IV antibiotics, followed by interval appendectomy. Operating early in this inflamed, friable field risks bowel injury, fistula and unplanned bowel resection.
why_wrong_block:
A. Open drainage is more invasive and is reserved for collections that cannot be reached percutaneously or when percutaneous drainage fails.
C. Removing the appendix now means dissecting through an inflamed, friable abscess cavity, with more complications (bowel injury, fistula, bowel resection); the appendix is taken out later as an interval procedure.
D. Laparoscopic appendectomy is right for uncomplicated appendicitis, but with an established abscess the appendix is removed later, after drainage.
key_concept:
Complicated appendicitis: match treatment to the CT finding.
  • Uncomplicated: laparoscopic appendectomy
  • Phlegmon (mass, no collection): IV antibiotics, conservative
  • Abscess: percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + interval appendectomy
  • Small collection: antibiotics alone
  • Unstable or generalized peritonitis: surgery
exam_pearl: Abscess is drained first and the appendix removed later; phlegmon is treated with antibiotics only.

stem: 70 years old, 4 days post knee replacement No symptoms only labs HR 115 Temp 38.9 WBC 15 Xray: right lower lobe infilteration What is the most appropriate “INITIAL” step in management? (BP NOT MENTIONED) (It Literally Said INITIAL , NOT NEXT)
key_concept:
Post-op fever: think by day, then treat the cause; shock always takes priority.
  • Days 1 to 2: wind (atelectasis, early pneumonia, aspiration)
  • Days 3 to 5: water (UTI, catheter or line infection)
  • Days 5 to 7: wound (surgical site infection); DVT/PE from about day 5
  • Fever + tachycardia + WBC + new infiltrate = pneumonia with SIRS
  • Hypotensive: fluids and antibiotics together, within the first hour
  • Normotensive: cultures then broad-spectrum antibiotics
exam_pearl: "Initial" with no BP stated: fluids only if you are told about hypotension or poor perfusion; otherwise the infection itself is treated.

stem: 22 year old female, has non tender, mobile, firm thyroid noqdule moves with tongue protrusion (She is not complaining of anything) US: Hypo echoic and inside it microcalcifications Size: 3 cm Most appropriate next step?
OptB: give thyroxine then reassess in 2 months
highlight_terms_source: Hypo echoic and inside it microcalcifications
why_right: A 3 cm nodule that is "hypoechoic" with "microcalcifications" has suspicious ultrasound features and is well above the size threshold for sampling, so the next step is FNA for cytology. Being young, asymptomatic and non-tender does not lower the concern; the ultrasound pattern decides. Cytology (Bethesda category) then dictates surgery or follow-up.
why_wrong_block:
B. TSH-suppressive thyroxine is not used to treat or shrink a suspicious nodule; it delays diagnosis of a possible carcinoma.
C. Discharge (or US follow-up) fits a sub-centimetre or purely benign-looking (e.g. spongiform, purely cystic) nodule; this one is 3 cm with malignant features.
D. Thyroidectomy follows cytology (e.g. suspicious or malignant Bethesda result) or compressive symptoms; operating before FNA skips the diagnosis.
key_concept:
Thyroid nodule workup: TSH + neck US, then decide on FNA.
  • Low TSH: scintigraphy (hot nodule rarely malignant)
  • Normal or high TSH: check FNA criteria
  • Suspicious US (hypoechoic, microcalcifications) ≥1 cm: FNA
  • Below criteria: US follow-up
  • FNA result (Bethesda) decides surgery
exam_pearl: If the stem gives a low TSH, the next step flips to a thyroid scan, not FNA.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Hypo-Echoic → FNA if 1 cm; if below 1 cm → Follow Up.

stem: diabetic patient presents with a foul-smelling ulcer. What is the most beneficial initial management step?
why_right: A "foul-smelling" diabetic ulcer implies infected, necrotic or sloughy tissue, and no wound heals or clears infection while dead tissue remains. Debridement is therefore the most beneficial initial step: it removes the bacterial load, lets you assess depth (bone, abscess) and obtain deep cultures. Every adjunct listed works only on a clean, debrided bed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Advanced dressings support a clean granulating wound after debridement; on necrotic, infected tissue they do not address the cause.
C. Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct for selected refractory or ischemic diabetic foot wounds that fail standard care, not a first step.
D. Negative pressure (VAC) therapy is for a non-healing wound or one at risk of non-healing, applied after debridement; it is contraindicated over untreated necrotic or grossly infected tissue.
key_concept:
Wound ladder: clean it first, then help it close.
  • Necrotic or foul tissue: debridement
  • Then secondary closure or grafting
  • Diabetic ulcer or bed sore at risk of non-healing: VAC after debridement
  • Infected diabetic foot: add antibiotics, check for osteomyelitis
  • HBOT: refractory cases only
exam_pearl: VAC is the answer only when the stem says the wound is already debrided or clean but not healing.

stem: post MI developed signs of DVT femoral pulse intact but all pulses below cannot be felt What is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: femoral pulse intact but all pulses below cannot be felt
why_right: "Femoral pulse intact but all pulses below cannot be felt" is acute arterial occlusion, not DVT (the "DVT" wording is almost certainly a recall slip). After an MI, a left ventricular mural thrombus is a classic embolic source, so this is an embolus lodged at the femoral bifurcation, and the definitive treatment of embolic acute limb ischemia is (Fogarty balloon) embolectomy. Heparin would be given immediately, but it is not among the options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral warfarin is for long-term prevention after the event (e.g. mural thrombus or AF); it does nothing for an acutely threatened limb. The acute anticoagulant would be IV heparin.
C. Angiography helps when the cause is unclear (e.g. thrombosis on chronic PAD with claudication history) and the limb is not immediately threatened; a clear embolic source with sudden loss of pulses goes straight to embolectomy, and imaging should not delay surgery if there is a motor or sensory deficit.
D. Catheter-directed thrombolysis suits in situ thrombosis on atherosclerotic disease or distal small-vessel occlusion in a viable limb; a fresh cardiac embolus at a proximal bifurcation is removed surgically, which is faster and more reliable.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: heparin first, then revascularize according to cause.
  • Embolic (AF, post-MI mural thrombus, no claudication history): embolectomy
  • Thrombotic (prior claudication, PAD risk factors): imaging, then thrombolysis or bypass
  • Irreversible limb (fixed paralysis, mottling): amputation
  • Pulse level localizes: femoral present, popliteal absent = femoral bifurcation or below
exam_pearl: "Next step" with heparin among the options: pick heparin; "definitive management" of an embolus: embolectomy.

stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic because his parents noticed that his asymptomatic small olive shape mass and . On examination, the right testis is not palpable in the scrotum. What is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: right testis is not palpable in the scrotum
why_right: A 2-year-old with the "right testis not palpable in the scrotum" has an undescended testis well past the age at which spontaneous descent can be expected (about 6 months). Surgery is ideally done by 18 months, so at 2 years it is already due and should be done now to protect fertility, reduce torsion risk and allow future examination for malignancy. A palpable undescended testis is brought down by orchidopexy; a truly non-palpable one is located by diagnostic laparoscopy, then fixed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Waiting until age 5 increases the risk of germ cell damage and infertility; delay is never preferred once the window for spontaneous descent has passed.
C. Observation fits a newborn or infant under about 6 months, when spontaneous descent still occurs, or a retractile testis that can be brought into the scrotum and stays there.
key_concept:
Undescended testis: operate early, not late.
  • Under about 6 months: observe for spontaneous descent
  • Orchidopexy ideally by 6 to 18 months
  • Palpable (e.g. inguinal canal): orchidopexy
  • Non-palpable: diagnostic laparoscopy
  • Hormonal therapy: not recommended
  • Post-pubertal unilateral: consider orchidectomy
exam_pearl: Retractile testis (can be manipulated into the scrotum and stays) needs only reassurance, not surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recall stem is garbled (mentions an 'olive shape mass'); compiler added a separate pyloric stenosis question after it (see 1340b).

stem: A 5-month-old baby was admitted with an inability to tolerate food and non-bilious vomiting over the past 2 days. On examination, he appears to be dehydrated. There is an olive-shaped mass palpable in the epigastric region measuring 2 × 2 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: olive-shaped mass palpable in the epigastric region
why_right: "Non-bilious vomiting", dehydration and a palpable "olive-shaped mass" in the epigastrium are hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. The definitive treatment is Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, splitting the hypertrophied muscle. It is not an emergency: dehydration and the hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis are corrected with normal saline (plus potassium) first, then surgery. The age of 5 months is older than typical (2 to 8 weeks), but the findings are classic.
why_wrong_block:
B. Balloon dilatation is used for acquired adult pyloric stenosis (e.g. peptic scarring); infantile muscular hypertrophy is cured by pyloromyotomy.
C. Gastrojejunostomy is a bypass for adult gastric outlet obstruction such as malignancy; it is unnecessary and more morbid in an infant.
key_concept:
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
  • First-born male, 2 to 8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting, hungry after
  • Olive mass, visible peristalsis left to right
  • Labs: hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis
  • Diagnosis: ultrasound
  • Step 1: fluids and electrolytes (normal saline)
  • Step 2: Ramstedt pyloromyotomy
exam_pearl: If the lead-in asks "immediate" or "initial" step, the answer is correcting dehydration and electrolytes, not pyloromyotomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's 'Q:' block under 1340 (unnumbered); a different question (pyloric stenosis).

stem: Qs about pediatric patient, I think the case was testicular torsion. Asking about golden hour for treatment.
why_right: Testicular torsion twists the spermatic cord and cuts off arterial inflow, so viability depends on time to detorsion. Salvage is highest when the testis is untwisted within about 6 hours of pain onset, which is why 6 hours is taught as the golden window. This is why a clinical diagnosis goes straight to scrotal exploration without waiting for imaging.
why_wrong_block:
B. 8 hours is already beyond the golden window; salvage falls progressively after 6 hours, although exploration is still performed.
C. By 12 hours salvage rates are much lower; this is not the window to aim for.
D. At 24 hours the testis is usually non-viable and often needs orchidectomy; still explore, but salvage is unlikely.
key_concept:
Torsion is a time-critical clinical diagnosis.
  • Sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
  • High suspicion: scrotal exploration, no imaging delay
  • Doppler US only if diagnosis uncertain
  • Surgery: detorsion + bilateral orchidopexy; orchidectomy if non-viable
  • Golden window: about 6 hours
exam_pearl: Torsion can present as lower abdominal pain only; always examine the scrotum in a boy with abdominal pain.

stem: Scenario about testicular torsion, imaging of choice:
why_right: When imaging is used for suspected torsion, the study of choice is scrotal Doppler ultrasound: it is fast, bedside, radiation-free and shows absent or reduced flow to the affected testis. Remember the order of priorities: torsion is a clinical diagnosis, and with high suspicion the patient goes to exploration without imaging; Doppler is reserved for uncertain cases.
why_wrong_block:
A. Plain X-ray cannot show the testis or its blood flow; it has no role in scrotal pain.
B. MRI can show testicular perfusion but is slow and not readily available, so it wastes the ischemic window.
D. CT exposes the gonads to radiation and does not assess testicular flow; CT suits renal colic or abdominal pathology, not the scrotum.
key_concept:
Acute scrotum: Doppler pattern separates the causes.
  • Torsion: absent or reduced flow; treat by exploration
  • Epididymo-orchitis: increased flow; antibiotics + NSAID
  • Torsion of appendix testis: upper pole pain, blue dot sign; NSAID
  • Clear clinical torsion: skip imaging, go to surgery
exam_pearl: If "Scrotal exploration" appears as an option in a classic torsion case, it beats ultrasound.

stem: Patient presents with swelling, the overlying skin was erythematous and fluctuance after a minor injury. What is the next step in management?
why_right: "Fluctuance" under erythematous skin after a minor injury means a collected abscess, not just cellulitis. Pus in a closed cavity is not penetrated well by antibiotics, so source control by incision and drainage is the treatment and the next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics alone treat cellulitis (redness, warmth, no fluctuance); for an abscess they are only an adjunct after drainage when there is systemic illness, extensive surrounding cellulitis or immunosuppression.
C. A CBC does not change management of a localized abscess; it may help in a systemically unwell patient, but drainage is still needed.
key_concept:
Skin and soft tissue infection: is there pus?
  • Redness, warmth, no fluctuance: cellulitis, antibiotics
  • Fluctuant collection: incision and drainage
  • Breast abscess, small with healthy skin: needle aspiration
  • Crepitus, rapid spread, severe pain: necrotizing infection, surgical debridement
exam_pearl: No fluctuance = cellulitis = antibiotics; fluctuance = abscess = drain it.

stem: A 46-year-old man, whose father was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer, comes for advice on screening. On digital rectal examination, the prostate is smooth, regular, and the sulcus is palpable. What is the next best step in management?
highlight_terms_source: father was recently diagnosed with prostate cancer
smooth, regular, and the sulcus is palpable
key_concept:
Prostate screening start depends on risk.
  • Average risk: shared decision from about 50
  • First-degree relative diagnosed before 65, or Black: from about 45
  • Several relatives diagnosed young: earlier still
  • Screening test: PSA (DRE only as adjunct)
  • Abnormal DRE or raised PSA: further evaluation (MRI, biopsy)
exam_pearl: Same stem, different key: father diagnosed young or Black patient means PSA; father diagnosed old means reassurance.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Compiler rule: If his father diagnosed before age of 65: B) PSA in 2 week. If father diagnosed after age of 65: A) reassurance. If he is Black: B) PSA in 2 week (regardless of family hx). Father's age not given in this recall, so no option marked. See 1356b/1356c variants (father 73 / 76: Reassurance).
⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 42-year-old male screened for prostate cancer. Father had prostate cancer at age 73. DRE mid? and soft. Most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: Father had prostate cancer at age 73
why_right: A 42-year-old with no symptoms and a soft prostate on DRE has no finding that needs work-up. His father was diagnosed at 73, i.e. after 65, so he does not count as a high-risk family history and he is below the usual age for average-risk screening discussion. Reassurance is therefore the most appropriate management.
why_wrong_block:
A. Immediate biopsy is reserved for an abnormal DRE (hard, nodular, asymmetric gland) or a raised PSA; this gland is soft and he has no PSA result.
C. Routine yearly DRE is not recommended as a screening tool in an average-risk man this young; screening, when chosen, is a shared decision based on PSA at an older age.
key_concept:
Prostate cancer screening depends on age and true risk, not on any family history.
  • Average risk: shared decision on PSA screening from about age 50 to 55
  • High risk (first-degree relative diagnosed before 65, or Black ethnicity): start earlier, around 40 to 45
  • Relative diagnosed after 65: treat as average risk
  • Hard or nodular DRE, or raised PSA: proceed to imaging and biopsy
exam_pearl: The age of the relative at diagnosis is the trap: a father diagnosed before 65 would change the answer toward early PSA screening.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's 'Q:' variant under 1356; options printed as A, B, D (third option lettered D in source). Father diagnosed after 65: reassurance.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the primary care clinic concerned about prostate cancer because his father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 76. The patient is completely asymptomatic with no urinary complaints. On digital rectal examination (DRE), the prostate is soft, smooth, of normal size, and the medial sulcus is easily palpable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at the age of 76
soft, smooth, of normal size, and the medial sulcus is easily palpable
why_right: This 45-year-old is completely asymptomatic and has a soft, smooth, normal-sized prostate with a preserved median sulcus, so the exam is normal. His father was diagnosed at 76, after age 65, which does not make him high risk. With no indication for testing, reassurance is the most appropriate next step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Annual DRE is not a recommended screening strategy and adds nothing for an average-risk man with a normal examination.
B. Transrectal ultrasound is used to guide biopsy or assess gland size, not to screen an asymptomatic man with a normal DRE.
D. PSA testing would be offered to a high-risk man at this age (relative diagnosed before 65) or to an average-risk man at an older age after shared decision making; neither applies here.
key_concept:
Normal DRE + no symptoms + relative diagnosed after 65 = average risk, reassure.
  • Abnormal DRE: hard, nodular, obliterated median sulcus
  • Early PSA screening only if first-degree relative diagnosed before 65 or other high-risk group
  • TRUS is a biopsy guide, not a screening test
exam_pearl: If the stem changes the father's age at diagnosis to under 65, PSA testing becomes the answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's second 'Q:' variant under 1356.

stem: 10yo boy with large swelling on the left side of his neck. On examination: 10 cm in size, soft and spongy. US FNA: clear lymphatic fluid. What is the appropriate management?
why_right: A soft, spongy lateral neck swelling in a child with clear lymphatic fluid on aspiration is a cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation). A 10 cm lesion will not regress and risks airway compression, infection and bleeding, so it needs active treatment. Of the listed options, surgical excision is the only definitive treatment.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation is acceptable only for small, asymptomatic lymphatic malformations; a 10 cm mass needs treatment.
C. Chemotherapy treats malignant neck masses such as lymphoma, which would give lymphoid cells on FNA rather than clear lymphatic fluid.
D. Radiotherapy has no role in a benign lymphatic malformation in a child and carries growth and malignancy risks.
key_concept:
Cystic hygroma = lateral, soft, transilluminant neck mass with clear lymphatic fluid.
  • Thyroglossal cyst: midline, moves with tongue protrusion, surgery (Sistrunk)
  • Branchial cyst: anterior border of sternocleidomastoid, cholesterol crystals
  • Cystic hygroma treatment: sclerotherapy, then surgery
exam_pearl: If sclerotherapy appears as an option it is usually preferred first for a macrocystic lesion; without it, surgery is the answer.

stem: Diabetic patient come with lateral leg ulcer, warm leg and there is discharge and black base and pulseless in distal dorsalis. The most likely cause is:
why_right: This recall's key is venous, most likely reflecting the lateral leg location, the warm leg and the discharge (exudate), all of which fit venous ulceration. However, the stem also says pulseless dorsalis pedis and a black base, which are the textbook features of an arterial ulcer. The card is kept as keyed, but compare it with the near-identical recall where the pulse is intact.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neuropathic ulcers sit on pressure points of the sole (metatarsal heads, heel) in a warm foot with palpable pulses and loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
C. Malignancy (Marjolin ulcer) is suspected in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled or everted edges; nothing here suggests it.
D. Arterial ulcers have absent pulses, a cold limb and a deep, punched-out, necrotic (black) base; the cold limb is missing here, but the absent pulse and black base point this way.
key_concept:
Leg ulcer: check the pulse first.
  • Absent pulse: arterial ulcer, arterial Doppler
  • Intact pulse: venous ulcer, venous duplex
  • Venous: gaiter area, shallow, irregular edge, pink granulating base, exudate, pigmentation
  • Arterial: pressure or trauma sites, punched out, deep, necrotic or sloughy base, cold limb
  • Neuropathic: plantar pressure points, painless, warm foot, pulses present
exam_pearl: In exam stems the distal pulse decides: absent = arterial, intact = venous.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Page marks Venous despite 'pulseless' in the stem (compare 1379, same options with intact pulse).

stem: 36 y/o male DM came complaining of ulcer in the medial site of the foot. WOTF is the highest risk of this ulcer?
highlight_terms_source: ulcer in the medial site of the foot
why_right: The key reads this as an ulcer over the medial aspect of the ankle/foot, the gaiter region, which is the classic site of venous ulceration. Venous ulcers result from sustained venous hypertension caused by valve incompetence, so venous hypertension is the strongest risk factor for an ulcer at this site. The patient is also young (36), making atherosclerotic disease less likely.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diabetes mainly causes neuropathic ulcers over plantar pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel) and contributes to arterial disease; it is not the main driver of a medial gaiter ulcer.
B. Atherosclerosis causes arterial ulcers on distal pressure or trauma sites (toes, heel, lateral malleolus) with absent pulses and pain, usually in older smokers.
key_concept:
Ulcer site points to the cause.
  • Medial malleolus / gaiter area: venous (venous hypertension)
  • Toes, heel, lateral malleolus, shin: arterial
  • Plantar metatarsal heads: neuropathic (diabetes)
exam_pearl: If the stem places the ulcer on the sole over a pressure point in a diabetic, the answer flips to diabetes (neuropathy).

stem: Diabetic patient come with lateral leg ulcer, warm leg and there is discharge and black base (in my exam there was sign of epithelization or something like that) and pulse is intact distal dorsalis (and another pulse also intact). The most likely cause is:
why_right: The deciding clue is the intact dorsalis pedis (and other distal pulses): a leg ulcer with intact pulses is treated as venous. A warm leg, discharge (exudate) and signs of epithelialisation also fit a venous ulcer. Even in a diabetic, intact pulses point to venous disease, and the next step would be venous duplex.
why_wrong_block:
A. Neuropathic ulcers occur over plantar pressure points with loss of sensation, not on the lateral leg.
C. Malignant change (Marjolin ulcer) is considered in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled edges or rapid growth; epithelialisation argues against it.
D. Arterial ulcers require absent or reduced pulses and a cold limb; here the pulses are intact and the leg is warm.
key_concept:
Leg ulcer first step = check distal pulses.
  • Intact pulse: venous, venous duplex
  • Absent pulse: arterial, arterial Doppler / ABI
  • Diabetes does not override the pulse finding
exam_pearl: Same options with a pulseless foot would point to arterial; the pulse is the switch.

stem: 45 y old came with severe pain during and after defecation, along with bright red blood on toilet paper, on examination posterior midline tear in the anal canal with increased sphincter tone. Most appropriate initial treatment?
highlight_terms_source: severe pain during and after defecation
bright red blood on toilet paper
posterior midline tear in the anal canal
why_right: Severe pain during and after defecation, bright red blood on the paper and a posterior midline tear with increased sphincter tone are classic for an anal fissure. The lead-in is initial treatment, which is medical: stool softeners and fibre plus a topical agent that relaxes the internal sphincter (chemical sphincterotomy), such as topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem.
why_wrong_block:
A. Colonoscopy is not needed for a typical midline fissure; it is indicated for atypical (lateral or multiple) fissures suggesting Crohn disease, or for red flags like age-related cancer risk.
C. Lateral internal sphincterotomy is for chronic fissures (over 6 weeks, sentinel tag) that fail medical therapy, not the initial step.
D. Antibiotics treat perianal abscess or infection (fever, fluctuant swelling, discharge), which is not present here.
key_concept:
Anal fissure: sharp pain on defecation + fresh blood + posterior midline tear.
  • All: fibre, fluids, stool softeners, sitz baths
  • Acute (under 6 weeks) or initial: topical nitrates or calcium channel blocker (diltiazem)
  • Refractory: botulinum toxin injection
  • Chronic failing medical therapy: lateral internal sphincterotomy
exam_pearl: Painless bleeding suggests hemorrhoids; painful bleeding with a midline tear is a fissure, and surgery only comes after medical failure.

stem: Pt post thyroid surg prez w numbness around lips and other hypocalcemia symptoms. Stated "Chovsteks sign". What's the cause?
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy complication by presentation.
  • Neck swelling + stridor within hours: hematoma, bedside wound exploration
  • Perioral numbness, spasm, Chvostek/Trousseau: hypocalcaemia, check calcium and replace
  • Hypocalcaemia refractory to replacement: check magnesium
  • Hoarseness, aspiration: recurrent laryngeal nerve
  • Loss of high pitch: superior laryngeal nerve
exam_pearl: Chvostek and Trousseau signs mean calcium, not nerve injury, even though both follow thyroid surgery.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient in hypovolemic shock, what do you monitor?
why_right: In hypovolemic shock the best bedside marker of end-organ perfusion and adequacy of resuscitation is urine output, monitored hourly via a urinary catheter. It reflects renal perfusion and falls progressively with each class of hemorrhage, so a target urine output is used to guide fluid resuscitation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Blood pressure is maintained by compensation and only falls once about 30 to 40% of volume is lost, so a normal BP can hide ongoing hypoperfusion.
C. Heart rate is an early sign but is unreliable as a resuscitation endpoint: it is blunted by beta blockers, age or pacemakers and raised by pain or anxiety.
key_concept:
Resuscitation adequacy = organ perfusion, best tracked by hourly urine output.
  • Class I: urine output normal
  • Class II: tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, BP normal, urine output mildly reduced
  • Class III: BP first drops, urine output markedly reduced
  • Class IV: urine output negligible
exam_pearl: BP is the last vital sign to fall in hemorrhage, so it is a poor monitor; urine output is the classic answer.
compiler_note: Compiler note: In hypovolemic shock, the most reliable indicator of adequate tissue perfusion and resuscitation is urine output. (Recall marked B with '??'.)

stem: Post total thyroidectomy (4 days) c/o of stridor and cough and SOB; upon inspection the nerve was damaged or stuck, I don't recall much. What's the management
why_right: This recall's key is cricothyroidotomy, read as the need for an immediate surgical airway in a patient with stridor and SOB after total thyroidectomy, where bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leaves both cords near the midline and obstructs the airway. The source itself is debated: laryngoscopy is the step that confirms cord palsy, and tracheostomy is the definitive airway for persistent bilateral palsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tracheostomy is the definitive airway when bilateral cord palsy persists; it is a planned procedure rather than the crash airway, which is why the source split on it.
B. Laryngoscopy confirms vocal cord paralysis and is the answer when the lead-in asks for the initial or next diagnostic step in a stable patient.
D. Repair of the recurrent laryngeal nerve is done only when a transection is recognised during surgery; it is not the management of airway compromise days later.
key_concept:
Post-thyroidectomy stridor: match the timing and the lead-in.
  • Hours post-op + neck swelling: hematoma, open the wound at the bedside
  • Stridor from bilateral RLN palsy: secure airway (intubation), surgical airway if intubation fails
  • Confirm palsy: laryngoscopy
  • Persistent bilateral palsy: tracheostomy
  • Unilateral RLN injury: hoarseness, aspiration, usually no stridor
exam_pearl: Read the verb: diagnosis or next step = laryngoscopy; definitive airway = tracheostomy; emergency when intubation fails = cricothyroidotomy.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: If asking about initial/next: Laryngoscopy to confirm the diagnosis of recurrent LN injury. If asking about definitive: Tracheostomy.
Other marked answers: Compiler explanation: B. Laryngoscopy (initial/next); Compiler explanation: A. Tracheostomy (definitive)

stem: Pt complains of bulge in his anus with fever, don't remember
why_right: The decisive clue is fever with a perianal bulge. A painful perianal swelling plus systemic signs of infection (fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis) is a perianal abscess, which needs incision and drainage.
why_wrong_block: B. Thrombosed pile: a very painful, tender bluish swelling at the anal verge, usually after straining or constipation, and the patient is typically afebrile. Here the fever points to infection, not thrombosis.
key_concept:
Perianal swelling: fever or not decides.
  • Painful swelling + fever ± high WBC: perianal abscess, incision and drainage
  • Painful tender bluish swelling, afebrile: thrombosed external pile
  • Sharp pain with defecation, fresh blood, no swelling: anal fissure
  • Chronic discharging opening after an abscess burst: fistula in ano
exam_pearl: Remove the fever and the same painful perianal lump becomes a thrombosed pile.

stem: A 36-year-old patient presented with a neck mass that has been present for 3 years. Physical examination confirmed a palpable left thyroid gland; with no palpable cervical lymph nodes. Neck Ultrasound: Left thyroid nodule occupying most of the left lobe, measures 3.4 x 3.8 cm and has mixed cystic and solid components, the right lobe is normal. Fine Needle Aspiration: Finding is coded as Bethesda IV (suspicious for follicular neoplasm). Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: FNA coded Bethesda IV (suspicious for follicular neoplasm) cannot separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma on cytology, because that needs capsular or vascular invasion seen on histology. The answer is a diagnostic lobectomy of the affected side: a left hemithyroidectomy, since the nodule is confined to the left lobe, the right lobe is normal and there are no nodes.
why_wrong_block:
A. Thyroid scan: used when TSH is low to look for a hot (autonomous) nodule before FNA. No suppressed TSH is given here and cytology is already available.
B. Total thyroidectomy: for Bethesda VI (malignant), medullary cancer, or bilateral disease. Here the disease is unilateral and not yet proven malignant, so removing the normal right lobe is overtreatment.
D. Repeat FNA: the step for Bethesda I (nondiagnostic) and Bethesda III. Repeating cytology for Bethesda IV will not resolve the question of invasion.
key_concept:
Bethesda category drives thyroid nodule management.
  • I nondiagnostic: repeat FNA
  • II benign: ultrasound follow up
  • III: repeat FNA
  • IV follicular neoplasm: hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy)
  • V: manage as IV or VI
  • VI malignant: (near) total thyroidectomy
exam_pearl: Follicular lesion on FNA means you need the capsule, so take the lobe; only Bethesda VI earns a total thyroidectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Recaller: not sure the recall was exactly this GB/MG one, but 100% sure it said Bethesda IV and asked for management.

stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with a groin swelling that appears when she stands and disappears when lying down. On examination, the swelling is located below and lateral to the Pubic Tubercle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: below and lateral to the Pubic Tubercle
key_concept:
Pubic tubercle rule for groin hernias.
  • Above and medial: inguinal (direct or indirect)
  • Below and lateral: femoral
  • Indirect vs direct: lateral vs medial to inferior epigastric vessels; deep ring occlusion controls indirect
  • Femoral: women, high strangulation risk, repair even if asymptomatic
exam_pearl: Women get inguinal hernias more often than femoral, so decide by the pubic tubercle, not by sex.

stem: Acute limb ischemia what is the risk for it?
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: embolus vs thrombosis.
  • Embolic: AF, recent MI, valve disease; sudden onset, normal other limb; treat with embolectomy
  • Thrombotic: prior claudication or PAD (smoking, diabetes); acute on chronic; catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Features: 6 Ps (pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis)
exam_pearl: If the option list includes AF, that is the classic answer for embolic acute limb ischemia; claudication history points to thrombosis.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Patient 2 months claudication pain, ABI was 0.3 CTA showed 3cm occlusion in popliteal artery, what's the most app step
key_concept:
Limb ischemia treatment fork.
  • Chronic claudication: exercise program, risk factor control, antiplatelet; revascularize if disabling or critical
  • Short focal lesion, viable limb: endovascular angioplasty or stenting
  • Long or diffuse lesion: surgical bypass
  • Acute embolic (AF): embolectomy
  • Acute thrombotic (on PAD): catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Nonviable limb: amputation
exam_pearl: Viability decides: a viable limb is revascularized, only a dead or unsalvageable limb is amputated.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Old patient long history of leg claudication *for 2 months*, present with leg pain and ABI <0.3 and, *CTA show artery occlusion more than 3 cm* what to do?
why_right: This recall's key is amputation because the scenario is framed as acute on chronic ischemia: a long history of claudication, new leg pain, an ABI below 0.3 and an occlusion longer than 3 cm. The teaching rule used for this question is that acute on chronic ischemia with ABI below 0.3 (or an irreversibly paralysed limb) is managed by amputation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Thrombolysis: chosen for acute on chronic in situ thrombosis when the limb is still salvageable; here the severity markers in the stem (ABI below 0.3, long occlusion) are used to signal an unsalvageable limb.
C. Embolectomy: for embolic acute ischemia (AF, recent MI) in a previously normal artery; this patient has long standing atherosclerotic disease, not an embolic source.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia treatment by cause.
  • Cardiac embolus (AF): embolectomy
  • In situ thrombosis on PAD: catheter directed thrombolysis
  • Acute on chronic with ABI below 0.3 or irreversible paralysis: amputation
  • Initial step in all: heparin
exam_pearl: Embolus means embolectomy, thrombosis means thrombolysis, nonviable limb means amputation.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot of another recall of the same scenario (see 1433) with printed Answer: A.

stem: 65 yo male came complaining with sudden lower fossa pain that is increasing. Labs: Wbc 23, Hb normal. CT shows diverticulitis + collection. What is the initial and most appropriate?
why_right: CT shows diverticulitis with a collection (a diverticular abscess, Hinchey I or II) and the stem does not describe generalized peritonitis or instability. A drainable abscess (about 4 cm or more) is treated with IV antibiotics plus image guided percutaneous drainage, which is both the initial and the most appropriate step.
why_wrong_block:
A. Laparoscopy: reserved for failed percutaneous drainage, an undrainable abscess, or purulent peritonitis (Hinchey III) where laparoscopic lavage or resection is considered.
B. Open laparotomy: for perforated diverticulitis with generalized (purulent or feculent) peritonitis, Hinchey III or IV, or an unstable patient; not for a contained, drainable collection.
key_concept:
Diverticulitis management by Hinchey stage.
  • Uncomplicated: antibiotics (or observation if mild and immunocompetent)
  • Small abscess (about 3 cm or less): IV antibiotics alone
  • Larger abscess (about 4 cm or more): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Purulent or feculent peritonitis: surgery (laparotomy, Hartmann)
  • After recovery: colonoscopy at 6 to 8 weeks to exclude cancer
exam_pearl: A contained collection is drained through the skin; free perforation with peritonitis goes to theatre.
compiler_note:
Terse recall of the same question: Diverticulitis with fluid collection about 20/13 cm what to do next??
Compiler note: Compiler typed 'A. Percutaneous drain.' under the recall. Rule: 4 cm -> drain; 3 cm -> conservative (if there is fever or SIRS, choose IV Abx over conservative). Options taken from the 'Diverticulosis with collection management' restatement.

stem: Q: Patient with acute diverticulitis fluid collection What is your next step
key_concept:
Diverticular collection: size and sepsis decide.
  • Small collection: IV antibiotics (conservative)
  • Larger collection (about 4 cm or more): percutaneous drainage + antibiotics
  • Generalized peritonitis: laparotomy
  • Colonoscopy: 6 to 8 weeks later, never in the acute phase
exam_pearl: Colonoscopy is the right answer only when the stem says the attack has resolved.

Compiler note: Additional version inside 1447 block; size of collection not stated. Rule given: 4 cm -> drain; 3 cm -> conservative, IV Abx if fever/SIRS.

stem: A 19-year-old man presented with a 3-day history of frequent attacks of per-rectal fresh bleeding. Physical examination confirmed clotted blood in the rectum. Nasogastric tube was draining greenish coloured fluids. Hb 85. Colonoscopy: no colorectal pathology. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic tool to localize source of bleeding?
why_right: A 19-year-old with painless recurrent fresh rectal bleeding, a nasogastric tube draining bile (greenish fluid) that argues against an upper GI source, and a normal colonoscopy points to a small bowel source, most likely a Meckel diverticulum. A technetium 99m pertechnetate (Meckel) scan localizes it by detecting ectopic gastric mucosa.
why_wrong_block:
A. Diagnostic laparoscopy: may be used to confirm and resect a Meckel diverticulum once suspected, but it is invasive and not the first test to localize bleeding.
B. Gastrografin follow through: a contrast study for obstruction or fistula; it does not show the bleeding point or the ectopic gastric mucosa.
C. Upper GI endoscopy: first line when an upper source is suspected (melena, blood in the NG aspirate); here bilious NG drainage makes an upper source unlikely.
key_concept:
Bleeding with negative colonoscopy: think small bowel.
  • Young, painless bright red bleeding: Meckel scan (Tc 99m pertechnetate)
  • Bilious NG aspirate without blood: upper source unlikely
  • Older, stable, negative EGD and colonoscopy: capsule endoscopy
  • Active brisk bleeding: CT angiography or tagged RBC scan
exam_pearl: Meckel rule of 2: about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, presents before age 2, may contain gastric or pancreatic tissue.

Terse recall of the same question: Young with 12 years age bloody diarrhea colonoscopy negative what next?
