stem: A 40-year-old diabetic patient complains of a painful perianal swelling with fever for the last 3 days (see lab results). Blood pressure: 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate: 110/min, Respiratory rate: 20/min, Temperature: 38 °C. Test Result Normal Values: Hb: 135 (130-170 g/L for Male, 120-160 g/L for Female), WBC: 16 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L), Neutrophils: 80 (40-60%), Random Glucose: 6.5 (3.9-5.5 mmol/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A painful perianal swelling for 3 days with fever 38 °C, tachycardia 110/min and leukocytosis (WBC 16, neutrophils 80%) is a perianal abscess. The systemic inflammatory response is the decisive clue that separates an infected collection from a simple painful lump. Diabetes is a classic risk factor for perianal sepsis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anal fissure causes sharp pain during and after defecation with fresh bleeding; there is no swelling, fever or raised WBC.
B. Internal hemorrhoids present with painless fresh bleeding after defecation, not a tender swelling with fever and leukocytosis.
D. Thrombosed piles give an acutely painful bluish swelling but the patient is afebrile with a normal WBC; fever plus neutrophilia points to pus.
key_concept:
Painful perianal lump: look at temperature and WBC first.
  • Lump + fever + leukocytosis = perianal abscess (incision and drainage)
  • Lump + normal vitals and WBC = perianal hematoma / thrombosed external pile
  • Pain on defecation + fresh blood, no lump = anal fissure
  • Painless fresh bleeding = internal hemorrhoids
  • Persistent discharge after a lump ruptured = fistula in ano
exam_pearl: Same painful lump but afebrile with normal WBC flips the answer to perianal hematoma.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Typed recall: "perianal abscess diagnosis clear". Compiler attached two screenshots on the next page (this one and a 30-year-old afebrile variant).

stem: A 30-year-old presented with a 3-day history of painful perianal swelling. Examination confirmed a 1x1 cm tender swelling close to the anal verge (see lab result). Heart rate 84/min, Temperature 37.2 °C. Test Result Normal Value: WBC 8 (4.5-10.5 x 10^9/L). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: 1x1 cm tender swelling close to the anal verge
why_right: A small (1x1 cm) tender swelling at the anal verge for 3 days in a patient with normal heart rate, temperature 37.2 °C and WBC 8 is a perianal hematoma (thrombosed external hemorrhoid). It is painful but there is no systemic inflammatory response, which rules out an abscess.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anal fissure is a linear tear giving sharp pain on defecation and bleeding; it does not produce a palpable swelling.
B. A prolapsed pile is a congested mucosal mass protruding from the anus, not a small tender subcutaneous lump at the verge.
C. Perianal abscess would come with fever, tachycardia and leukocytosis; here vitals and WBC are normal.
key_concept:
Painful perianal lump: vitals and WBC decide.
  • Normal temperature and WBC = perianal hematoma
  • Fever + leukocytosis = perianal abscess
  • Hematoma seen early (within about 72 h) can be evacuated; later it is managed conservatively
exam_pearl: Add fever and a raised WBC to the same lump and the answer becomes perianal abscess.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot under block 1731 (on next page); afebrile with normal WBC points away from abscess.

stem: Fournier's Gangrene DM crepitus and anal cellulitis initial investigation
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound can show subcutaneous gas or scrotal involvement, but it is operator dependent and does not change the need for immediate debridement once crepitus is felt.
B. MRI defines soft tissue extent well but is slow and often unavailable in the emergency setting; waiting for it delays life-saving surgery.
C. CT is the most useful imaging to map gas and the extent of spread in a stable patient when the diagnosis is unclear, but with clinical crepitus it should not postpone debridement.
key_concept:
Fournier gangrene = necrotizing fasciitis of the genitalia and perineum.
  • Risk: diabetes, immunosuppression, perianal or urogenital infection
  • Clues: pain out of proportion, crepitus, dusky skin, bullae, systemic toxicity
  • Polymicrobial (gram positive, gram negative, anaerobes)
  • Treatment: urgent surgical debridement + broad-spectrum IV antibiotics + resuscitation
  • Repeat debridement and later reconstruction as needed
exam_pearl: Crepitus in a diabetic perineum means theatre now; imaging is only for doubtful, stable cases.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Answer line gives Debridement (not among the listed options).

stem: Elderly, epigastric pain for 3m, wt loss, jaundice and dark urine There was dilatation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct Labs: cholestatic picture (They did not mention if the gallbladder is palpable or shrunk)
highlight_terms_source: wt loss, jaundice and dark urine
dilatation of intrahepatic and extrahepatic duct
why_right: An elderly patient with 3 months of epigastric pain, weight loss and obstructive jaundice (dark urine, cholestatic labs) suggests malignancy. Dilatation of both intrahepatic and extrahepatic ducts places the obstruction distally at the ampulla, so ampullary cancer fits best. The gallbladder status is not given, so the level of duct dilatation is the decisive clue.
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumor sits at the hepatic duct confluence, so only intrahepatic ducts dilate and the gallbladder is collapsed; extrahepatic dilatation excludes it.
B. Gallbladder cancer usually shows a gallbladder mass or wall thickening, often with gallstones, and causes jaundice by hilar invasion rather than a distal block with full-length duct dilatation.
key_concept:
Level of biliary dilatation localises the tumour.
  • Intrahepatic only + collapsed GB = Klatskin (hilar cholangiocarcinoma)
  • Intra + extrahepatic + distended GB = distal block (pancreatic head, ampullary, periampullary)
  • Palpable non-tender GB with jaundice = Courvoisier sign, favours malignancy over stones
exam_pearl: If only intrahepatic ducts are dilated, switch to Klatskin tumor.

stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-month history of yellowish discoloration of his sclera and skin with dark urine and pale stool. On examination, he was jaundiced with a palpable distended gallbladder (see report and lab results). Test Result Normal Values: Alkaline phosphatase 421 (39-117 IU/L), Direct bilirubin 122.3 (1.5-6.5 umol/L), Total bilirubin 134.5 (3.5-16.5 umol/L). Ultrasound: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Dilated intra and extrahepatic bile ducts with hugely distended gallbladder
why_right: A 67-year-old man with 2 months of jaundice, dark urine and pale stool has obstructive jaundice (ALP and direct bilirubin high). A palpable distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) plus dilated intra and extrahepatic ducts with a hugely distended gallbladder place a malignant block in the distal CBD, classically pancreatic head cancer.
why_wrong_block:
A. Klatskin tumor is at the hepatic duct confluence, giving a shrunken gallbladder and only intrahepatic dilatation.
C. Mirizzi syndrome is a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann pouch compressing the common hepatic duct, with RUQ pain and cholecystitis features, not painless progressive jaundice with a huge gallbladder.
D. CBD stones give painful, fluctuating jaundice and the gallbladder is usually fibrosed and not palpable (Courvoisier law).
key_concept:
Courvoisier law: jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be stones.
  • Distended GB + intra and extrahepatic dilatation = pancreatic head or periampullary tumour
  • Collapsed GB + intrahepatic dilatation only = Klatskin
  • Stones: pain, fluctuating jaundice, fibrosed GB
exam_pearl: Collapsed gallbladder with intrahepatic dilatation only flips the answer to Klatskin tumor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's "Q:" related version under 1745; Answer: B (MG).

stem: 42-year-old patient undergoes colonoscopy for evaluation of gastrointestinal symptoms. A 1.3 cm colonic polyp is identified and removed. Histopathology reveals a tubular adenoma. What is the most appropriate follow-up colonoscopy interval?
why_right: A single tubular adenoma of 1.3 cm is an advanced adenoma because it is ≥10 mm. Current post-polypectomy surveillance guidance recommends repeat colonoscopy at 3 years for an adenoma ≥10 mm after complete removal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ten years is the interval after a normal colonoscopy, or roughly 7 to 10 years for 1 to 2 small (<10 mm) tubular adenomas; a 1.3 cm adenoma is higher risk.
B. Very short intervals (months) are for incomplete or piecemeal removal of a large polyp, or a malignant polyp, not a completely excised tubular adenoma.
C. An adenoma is a premalignant neoplastic polyp, so surveillance colonoscopy is always needed after removal; even small hyperplastic polyps (<10 mm) still return to routine 10-year screening rather than no follow-up.
key_concept:
Surveillance depends on adenoma size, number and histology.
  • Normal colonoscopy: 10 years
  • 1 to 2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7 to 10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous histology or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal removal of a large polyp: early check in about 6 months
  • Malignant risk: villous > tubulovillous > tubular > hyperplastic
exam_pearl: Size ≥10 mm or villous/high-grade dysplasia makes it advanced: 3 years.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1828).

stem: 40~yr, Breast mass for 3 months upper outer quadrant Biopsy option
why_right: A 40-year-old with a 3-month upper outer quadrant breast mass is evaluated by triple assessment; the biopsy of choice for a solid breast mass is core needle (Tru-cut) biopsy. It gives histology with tissue architecture, distinguishes invasive from in situ disease and allows receptor testing before definitive surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. FNAC gives cytology only and cannot show invasion or receptor status; it is used for cystic lesions or axillary nodes.
C. Excisional biopsy is not first-line for a suspicious mass because it can compromise later definitive surgery; it is used when core biopsy is non-diagnostic or discordant, or for some benign lesions.
key_concept:
Triple assessment: clinical exam + imaging + biopsy.
  • Age >30: mammogram ± ultrasound first
  • Age <30: ultrasound first
  • Solid mass: core needle (Tru-cut) biopsy
  • Cystic mass: fine needle aspiration
exam_pearl: If the question asks the first step (not the biopsy), a woman over 30 gets imaging (mammogram) before biopsy.

stem: Man with pulsatile abdominal mass there's evidence of rupture: Asking about definitive management:
key_concept:
AAA: pulsatile supraumbilical mass, pain radiating to the back.
  • Unstable or suspected rupture: bedside ultrasound, straight to theatre
  • Stable and symptomatic: CT angiography
  • Repair if >5.5 cm in men, >5 cm in women, rapidly growing, symptomatic or ruptured
  • Small asymptomatic: surveillance
exam_pearl: Rupture means repair; drugs only buy time.

stem: 55 y/o Women with birad 0 The mammogram show overlaps shadows bilaterally what to do:
OptD: some surgical or biopsy for both breasts
why_right: BI-RADS 0 means the mammogram is incomplete: findings such as overlapping shadows cannot be categorised without more imaging. The correct action is further investigation (additional diagnostic mammographic views such as spot compression, and/or ultrasound), then assigning a final BI-RADS category.
why_wrong_block:
A. Short-interval (6-month) follow-up is for BI-RADS 3, probably benign; a BI-RADS 0 study has no final category yet.
B. Routine yearly or screening-interval mammography is for BI-RADS 1 or 2 (negative or benign).
D. Biopsy is for BI-RADS 4 or 5 lesions; overlapping tissue shadows do not justify bilateral tissue sampling before work-up is complete.
key_concept:
BI-RADS actions:
  • 0: incomplete, additional imaging
  • 1 to 2: negative or benign, routine screening
  • 3: probably benign, short-interval follow-up (about 6 months)
  • 4 to 5: suspicious or highly suggestive, core needle biopsy
  • 6: known malignancy, treat
exam_pearl: BI-RADS 0 is not a result; it is a request for more imaging.

stem: Patient after MVA has severe back pain, exam is normal, respiration is normal Neurosurgical consult is ordered What measures is best now
key_concept:
Suspected spinal injury: protect first, then image.
  • High energy mechanism + midline back or neck pain = assume spinal injury.
  • Maintain immobilization (log roll, collar) until cleared.
  • CT is the imaging of choice to clear the spine.
  • MRI if neurological deficit or suspected cord or ligament injury.
  • A normal neuro exam does not exclude an unstable fracture.
exam_pearl: "Best measure now" in a stable patient awaiting a consult points to protection (immobilization); "best test" points to CT.

stem: 21 year old patient with right iliac fossa pain for 7 days on examination: palpable mass at the iliac fossa WBC high US done showing appendiceal mass with Collection What to do:
why_right: Pain for 7 days with a palpable RIF mass means the appendix has already been walled off (an appendiceal mass, here with a collection). Operating early in this setting is hazardous because of dense inflammatory adhesions, so the first line is non-operative care: IV antibiotics, fluids and close monitoring, with appendectomy deferred. This recall's key is non interventional management because it is the only option that avoids immediate surgery.
why_wrong_block:
B. Laparoscopic appendectomy is for acute uncomplicated appendicitis presenting early; with a 7 day history and a formed mass, operating risks bowel injury and fistula.
C. Open appendectomy has the same problem as laparoscopy in a late presentation with a mass; it is not the first step for an appendiceal mass or abscess.
D. Exploratory laparotomy is for generalized peritonitis or an unstable patient; this patient has a localized mass.
key_concept:
Late appendicitis with a mass is treated non-operatively first.
  • Early uncomplicated appendicitis: laparoscopic appendectomy.
  • Phlegmon (mass, no collection): IV antibiotics, conservative.
  • Abscess (collection): percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics, then interval appendectomy.
  • Small collection: antibiotics alone may suffice.
  • Generalized peritonitis or instability: operate.
  • Older patient after recovery: colonoscopy to exclude malignancy.
exam_pearl: Days of pain plus a palpable mass flips the answer away from appendectomy toward non-operative care.

stem: Man with inguinal hernia with mild pain
why_right: An inguinal hernia causing mild pain is symptomatic, so it should be repaired. Tension-free mesh repair (open mesh, e.g. Lichtenstein, for a primary unilateral hernia) is the standard because it has the lowest recurrence.
why_wrong_block:
A. Bassini is a tissue (suture) repair under tension with higher recurrence than mesh; it is reserved for when mesh cannot be used, such as a contaminated field.
C. Watchful waiting suits a painless (asymptomatic) hernia in a man who prefers to avoid surgery; this hernia already causes pain, so elective repair is advised.
key_concept:
Symptomatic inguinal hernia = elective mesh repair.
  • Primary unilateral: open mesh repair.
  • Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic mesh repair.
  • Faster recovery needed: laparoscopic.
  • Strangulated or large complex hernia: open repair.
  • Tissue repair (Bassini, Shouldice) only if mesh is not suitable.
exam_pearl: Recurrent or bilateral flips the answer from open mesh to laparoscopic mesh.

stem: splenic laceration grade3 : whats management :
key_concept:
Splenic injury: stability decides, not the grade.
  • Stable: non-operative management with monitoring.
  • Stable with contrast blush: angioembolization.
  • Unstable or peritonitis: splenectomy (laparotomy).
  • Failure of observation (falling Hb, instability): operate.

stem: A 36-year-old man was stabbed in the right lower quadrant of his abdomen 1 hour back. He complained of pain at the wound site. Local wound exploration revealed penetration of the anterior abdominal fascia. Blood pressure 110/62 mmHg Heart rate 87 /min Temperature 37.2 °C Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
highlight_terms_source: stabbed in the right lower quadrant
penetration of the anterior abdominal fascia
why_right: The patient is hemodynamically stable (BP 110/62, HR 87, afebrile) after a stab wound, and the only finding is anterior fascial penetration on local exploration. Fascial breach alone is not a laparotomy indication, so a stable abdominal trauma patient is evaluated with CT abdomen to look for peritoneal violation and organ injury.
why_wrong_block:
B. Observation alone ignores a known fascial breach; serial exams can be part of care, but the next step here is to define the injury with CT.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy is invasive; it is used when CT is equivocal or to look for diaphragmatic or peritoneal injury, not as the first step in a stable patient.

key_concept:

  • Stable: CT abdomen.
  • Unstable stab wound: laparotomy.
  • Peritonitis, evisceration, omentum in wound: laparotomy.
  • Unstable blunt trauma: FAST; positive leads to laparotomy.
  • Positive CT findings: laparotomy.
exam_pearl: Add hypotension, peritonitis or evisceration and the answer flips to laparotomy.

stem: Elderly diabetic, black toe, dorsalis absent/not palpable, next or initial management:
why_right: An elderly diabetic with a black toe (gangrene) and an absent dorsalis pedis pulse has suspected critical limb ischemia. The first investigation is the ankle brachial index, a bedside non-invasive test that confirms and grades arterial disease before duplex, CT angiography and revascularization planning.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tissue biopsy is for a chronic non-healing ulcer suspected of malignant change; gangrene from ischemia is diagnosed by vascular assessment, not histology.
C. MRI is for suspected osteomyelitis under a diabetic foot ulcer; it does not assess arterial perfusion, which is the issue with a black toe and absent pulse.
key_concept:
Ischemic foot work-up ladder.
  • Step 1: ABI.
  • Step 2: arterial duplex ultrasound.
  • Step 3: CT angiography to plan revascularization.
  • Calcified vessels in diabetes can falsely raise ABI; use toe pressures if so.
  • Probe to bone or suspected osteomyelitis: X ray then MRI.
exam_pearl: A falsely high or normal ABI in a diabetic with absent pulses means calcified arteries, not a normal circulation.

stem: What's would decrease if patient loss 25% of their blood volume
why_right: Losing 25% of blood volume is class II hemorrhage (15 to 30%). In class II, compensatory vasoconstriction keeps systolic BP normal but raises diastolic pressure, so the pulse pressure narrows; it is the first pressure parameter to fall.
why_wrong_block:
B. Urine output in class II is only mildly reduced and still close to normal; it falls clearly in class III and IV, so it is not the most expected change.
C. GCS is preserved in class II (mild anxiety only); confusion and lethargy appear in class III and IV.
D. Heart rate rises (tachycardia) with blood loss; it does not decrease.
key_concept:
Hemorrhagic shock classes by % volume lost.
  • I (up to 15%): near normal vitals.
  • II (15 to 30%): tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, systolic BP normal.
  • III (30 to 40%): systolic BP falls, confusion, low urine output.
  • IV (over 40%): marked hypotension, negligible urine, lethargy.
exam_pearl: Systolic BP first drops in class III; if the loss is 30 to 40% the expected answer becomes hypotension.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot version: A trauma patient who lost 25% of his blood volume. Which of the following is most expected to be decreased? A. Urine output B. Pulse pressure C. Respiratory rate D. Glasco coma scale. Answer: B (Pulse pressure).

stem: Testicular torsion full symptoms & exam & U/S Clinical picture The Q asking for Tx
OptB: detwist the testicle + If pain relief discharge
why_right: The stem gives the full clinical picture plus exam and U/S of testicular torsion and asks for treatment. Torsion is a surgical emergency: the definitive management is urgent scrotal exploration with detorsion and orchiopexy (fixing the contralateral testis too), ideally within about 6 hours of pain onset to save the testis.
why_wrong_block: B. Detwist the testicle and discharge if pain relief: manual detorsion is only a temporizing bedside manoeuvre while theatre is arranged; pain relief does not guarantee full untwisting, and the patient still needs surgical exploration and bilateral fixation, never discharge.
key_concept:
Suspected testicular torsion = surgery, not imaging or observation.
  • Picture: sudden severe pain, high-riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex
  • Doppler only if the diagnosis is uncertain (absent flow); never delay theatre for it
  • Treatment: scrotal exploration + detorsion + bilateral orchiopexy
  • Torsion of appendage (blue dot, upper pole pain): conservative with NSAIDs
  • Epididymo-orchitis (increased flow): antibiotics + analgesia
exam_pearl: Manual detorsion with relief of pain still ends in the operating room; a discharge option in a torsion stem is always the trap.

stem: Trauma patient with hypotension, X-Ray reveled: Trachea shifted to the right, expanded lungs and widened mediastinum. What is the diagnosis?
why_right: A trauma patient with hypotension and a widened mediastinum has a traumatic aortic injury until proven otherwise. The mediastinal hematoma pushes the trachea to the right, a classic X-ray sign of aortic rupture, while expanded lungs rule out a large hemothorax or pneumothorax as the cause. Confirm with CT angiography if the patient can be stabilized.
why_wrong_block:
A. Massive hemothorax: would show a whited-out hemithorax with dull percussion and a collapsed lung, not expanded lungs with an isolated wide mediastinum.
B. Pneumothorax: shows absent lung markings and a collapsed lung; the lungs here are expanded. A tension pneumothorax would shift the trachea away from a hyperresonant side, not widen the mediastinum.
D. Spontaneous pneumothorax: by definition occurs without trauma (typically a tall thin smoker with a ruptured bleb) and would not explain the widened mediastinum.
key_concept:
Blunt chest trauma + widened mediastinum = aortic injury.
  • Other X-ray clues: tracheal or NG tube deviation to the right, loss of aortic knob, apical cap, left hemothorax
  • Stable: CT angiography; unstable: bedside echo (TEE)
  • Tension pneumothorax: hyperresonance, absent breath sounds, trachea away, raised JVP
  • Massive hemothorax: dullness, collapsed lung, more than 1500 ml on chest tube = thoracotomy
exam_pearl: Expanded lungs on the X-ray remove both pneumothorax and hemothorax; what is left with a wide mediastinum is the aorta.

stem: Pt post lap chole, next morning developed productive cough + high temperature Most appropriate next step?
why_right: Fever with a productive cough on the next morning after surgery (postoperative day 1) is classically due to atelectasis: post-anaesthesia hypoventilation and splinting from upper abdominal port pain cause retained secretions and alveolar collapse. Treatment is to re-expand the lung with chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry, early mobilisation and adequate analgesia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Observation: the collapse will not resolve without active lung expansion and can progress to pneumonia, so doing nothing is wrong.
B. CT scan: not needed for day 1 fever with a chest picture; CT is for suspected intra-abdominal collection, leak or abscess, which typically appear later (around day 5 onward).
C. Sputum culture: fits a postoperative pneumonia, which usually appears from about day 3 with consolidation; on day 1 the cause is atelectasis, not infection.
key_concept:
Postoperative fever by timing (the classic 'W' ladder).
  • Day 1-2: atelectasis (Wind) = chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry
  • Day 3-5: pneumonia, UTI (Water), phlebitis
  • Day 5-7: wound infection, anastomotic leak
  • Day 7+: DVT/PE, deep abscess (CT)
  • Very early (hours): malignant hyperthermia, transfusion reaction, necrotizing infection
exam_pearl: Same symptoms, different day: fever and cough on day 1 = atelectasis (physio); on day 3-5 = pneumonia (cultures, antibiotics).

stem: A diabetic pt has ulcer in lateral foot with discharge and granulation but intact pulse
why_right: This recall's key is venous ulcer, following the rule ulcer + intact pulse = venous (absent pulse = arterial), with a granulating, discharging base that fits the moist, pink base of a venous ulcer. On this teaching, the diabetes is a distractor once the pulses are confirmed present.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ischemic: arterial ulcers have absent or weak pulses, a punched-out painful ulcer with a pale, sloughy or necrotic base, not healthy granulation; the pulses here are intact.
C. Malignant: suspect a Marjolin (squamous cell) change in a long-standing non-healing ulcer with rolled everted edges, rapid growth or bleeding; biopsy then. Nothing here suggests it.
D. Neuropathic: the classic diabetic foot ulcer, painless over pressure points (metatarsal heads, heel, lateral border over the 5th metatarsal) with intact pulses and reduced sensation; the strongest competing answer for a diabetic foot.
key_concept:
Leg/foot ulcer approach: feel the pulses first.
  • Absent pulse: arterial ulcer, punched out, painful, necrotic base: arterial Doppler
  • Intact pulse + gaiter area, pigmentation, edema, granulating base: venous: venous duplex
  • Intact pulse + diabetic, pressure point, painless, callus, loss of sensation: neuropathic
  • Chronic non-healing with rolled edge: biopsy for Marjolin ulcer
exam_pearl: Site decides between venous and neuropathic: medial malleolus/gaiter area = venous; plantar or pressure areas of a diabetic foot = neuropathic.

stem: female had head injury presenting with to ED with GCS 8/15, with dark ecchymosis around the eyes and crusted blood in her nose nostril. What is the best way to secure her airway?
highlight_terms_source: crusted blood in her nose nostril
why_right: GCS 8 is an indication for a definitive airway. Dark ecchymosis around the eyes (raccoon eyes) and blood in the nostrils point to a basilar skull fracture, which contraindicates anything passed through the nose. So the airway is secured by orotracheal intubation (rapid sequence, with in-line cervical spine stabilization).
why_wrong_block:
B. Nasotracheal intubation: contraindicated with a suspected base of skull fracture (raccoon eyes, nasal bleeding, CSF rhinorrhea) because the tube can pass through the cribriform plate into the cranium; it is also a blind technique.
C. Cricothyroidotomy: the surgical rescue airway when oral intubation fails or is impossible, for example severe maxillofacial or mandibular injury with profuse oral bleeding; the mouth route here is usable.
D. Tracheostomy: a slow, elective or semi-elective procedure for prolonged ventilation or upper airway obstruction, not the emergency airway in the trauma bay.
key_concept:
Trauma airway: intubate for GCS ≤8, SpO2 <88%, unconsciousness or aspiration risk; then choose the route.
  • Default: orotracheal intubation with C-spine protection
  • Basilar skull fracture (raccoon eyes, Battle sign, CSF leak, hemotympanum): avoid nasal tubes
  • Severe facial/mandibular injury or failed intubation: cricothyroidotomy
  • Tracheostomy: not an emergency trauma airway
exam_pearl: Raccoon eyes do not push you to a surgical airway; they only forbid the nose. Facial bone destruction is what pushes you to cricothyroidotomy.

stem: A 40 to 45 year-old man undergoes colonoscopy, which reveals a polyp in the colon. Histopathologic examination shows a tubular adenoma measuring 1.5 cm in size. During the procedure, the surgeon remove 1.3 cm of the lesion. When should the next colonoscopy screening be performed?
why_right: The decisive clue is that the polyp measured 1.5 cm but the surgeon removed only 1.3 cm of it: the resection was incomplete and residual adenoma is left behind. Incomplete or piecemeal removal of a large adenoma needs an early repeat colonoscopy within a few months (3-6 months) to clear the site, before any routine surveillance interval applies.
why_wrong_block:
B. Every 3 years: the correct interval for a completely removed tubular adenoma ≥10 mm (an advanced adenoma); it does not apply while residual polyp remains.
C. Every 5 years: matches screening with CT colonography or flexible sigmoidoscopy, or older intervals for small adenomas; too long for a partly removed large adenoma.
D. No screening needed: an adenoma is a precancerous lesion; a 40-45 year old with residual adenoma needs completion and surveillance.
key_concept:
After polypectomy: first ask whether removal was complete, then size, number and histology.
  • 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous features or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)
  • Small hyperplastic polyps or normal colonoscopy (average risk): 10 years
  • Stopping surveillance is a decision for old age or limited life expectancy, not a young adult with an adenoma
exam_pearl: Read the sizes: lesion size larger than the resected size means incomplete removal, which flips 3 years into a short-interval re-look.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1825).

stem: A 30-year-old man underwent a colonoscopy, during which a polyp was removed. When should the next colonoscopy be performed?
key_concept:
Surveillance interval = completeness + histology + size + number.
  • 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous features or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)
  • Small hyperplastic polyps or normal colonoscopy (average risk): 10 years
  • Stopping surveillance is a decision for old age or limited life expectancy, not a young adult with an adenoma
exam_pearl: With no size, number or histology given, decide by asking: was it complete, and was it an adenoma? Those two facts set the interval.

stem: A patient presented with infrequent anal bleeding did a colonoscopy that revealed one polyp size 1.5cm and a biopsy showed tubular adenoma 1.2 cm. Interval of colonoscopy?
why_right: This recall's key is 6 months. It reads the stem as a 1.5 cm polyp whose specimen measured only 1.2 cm (and was described as a biopsy), meaning the adenoma was not fully removed; residual or piecemeal-resected large adenomas are rechecked early, at about 6 months, to confirm complete clearance.
why_wrong_block:
A. No need: a tubular adenoma is precancerous and a patient with one needs surveillance; no follow up is never right here.
C. 3 years: the interval for a completely removed tubular adenoma ≥10 mm; it would be the answer if the whole polyp had been taken out in one piece.
D. 5-10 years: fits 1-2 small (<10 mm) completely removed tubular adenomas or average-risk screening, not a 1.2-1.5 cm adenoma.
key_concept:
After polypectomy: complete or not first, then size and histology.
  • 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous features or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)
  • Small hyperplastic polyps or normal colonoscopy (average risk): 10 years
  • Stopping surveillance is a decision for old age or limited life expectancy, not a young adult with an adenoma
exam_pearl: If the polyp was completely removed, a 1.2-1.5 cm tubular adenoma is 3 years; the short interval only applies when tissue was left behind.

stem: A 42 year patient came with mild PR bleeding, there is no history of anything, no DM, no HTN. Colonoscopy show: 1.5 cm polyp sigmoid. Histopathology: tubular adenoma (also described as benign-looking). Which of the following true about the follow up of endoscopy?
OptD: No need for follow up of endoscopy

Tubular adenoma ≥10 mm = advanced adenoma: 3 years if fully removed.

  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)

stem: 45 man, i forgot his presentations, he did a colonoscopy: Polyps It was resected. Histopathology: Polyp tubular adenoma. When he should do colonoscopy again? (They did not mention how many polyps, there was description of how he presented but it wasn't urgent critical)
why_right: This recall's key is 3 years: a tubular adenoma was found and resected, the presentation was not urgent, and the classic recall rule is that a resected adenoma is followed by surveillance colonoscopy at 3 years. The 3-year interval is exact when the adenoma is ≥10 mm, has villous features or high-grade dysplasia, or there were multiple adenomas.
why_wrong_block:
A. 3-6 months: reserved for incomplete or piecemeal removal or poor preparation; here the polyp was resected.
C. 10 years: the interval for a normal colonoscopy or small hyperplastic polyps in an average-risk adult; current guidance gives 7-10 years only for 1-2 small (<10 mm) tubular adenomas.
D. No need: an adenoma is precancerous, so a 45-year-old needs surveillance after its removal.
key_concept:
Resected adenoma = surveillance; interval set by size, number and histology.
  • 1-2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7-10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous features or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal or incomplete removal of a large polyp: short interval re-look (about 6 months)
  • Small hyperplastic polyps or normal colonoscopy (average risk): 10 years
  • Stopping surveillance is a decision for old age or limited life expectancy, not a young adult with an adenoma
exam_pearl: When the stem gives no size or number, the recall default for a resected adenoma is 3 years; a stated size under 10 mm with 1-2 polyps would push it to 7-10 years.

stem: 42-year-old patient undergoes colonoscopy for evaluation of gastrointestinal symptoms. A 1.3 cm colonic polyp is identified and removed. Histopathology reveals a tubular adenoma. What is the most appropriate follow-up colonoscopy interval?
why_right: A single tubular adenoma of 1.3 cm is an advanced adenoma because it is ≥10 mm. Current post-polypectomy surveillance guidance recommends repeat colonoscopy at 3 years for an adenoma ≥10 mm after complete removal.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ten years is the interval after a normal colonoscopy, or roughly 7 to 10 years for 1 to 2 small (<10 mm) tubular adenomas; a 1.3 cm adenoma is higher risk.
B. Very short intervals (months) are for incomplete or piecemeal removal of a large polyp, or a malignant polyp, not a completely excised tubular adenoma.
C. An adenoma is a premalignant neoplastic polyp, so surveillance colonoscopy is always needed after removal; even small hyperplastic polyps (<10 mm) still return to routine 10-year screening rather than no follow-up.
key_concept:
Surveillance depends on adenoma size, number and histology.
  • Normal colonoscopy: 10 years
  • 1 to 2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: 7 to 10 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous histology or high-grade dysplasia: 3 years
  • Piecemeal removal of a large polyp: early check in about 6 months
  • Malignant risk: villous > tubulovillous > tubular > hyperplastic
exam_pearl: Size ≥10 mm or villous/high-grade dysplasia makes it advanced: 3 years.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1746).

stem: Patient did sigmoid polyp resection on Histopathology found to be Tubular adenoma, when to do colonoscopy after procedure?
why_right: A tubular adenoma is a true neoplastic (premalignant) polyp, so after removal the patient enters colonoscopic surveillance rather than routine screening. Of the options offered, 3 years is the only genuine post-polypectomy surveillance interval; it is the interval for an advanced adenoma (≥10 mm, villous features or high grade dysplasia), and it is this recall's key for a resected tubular adenoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. 3 to 6 months: an early repeat is only for an incomplete or piecemeal removal of a large polyp, or a poor bowel preparation; nothing here suggests incomplete resection.
B. 6 months: same as above, reserved for checking the site after piecemeal excision of a large adenoma; a completely resected tubular adenoma does not need it.
C. Yearly: annual testing describes stool based screening (FIT), not colonoscopic surveillance after polypectomy; it is far too frequent for a benign adenoma.
key_concept:
Post-polypectomy surveillance is set by the adenoma's size, number and histology, not by symptoms.
  • 1 to 2 tubular adenomas <10 mm: long interval (about 7 to 10 years in current guidance; 5 to 10 in older ones)
  • 3 to 4 small tubular adenomas: 3 to 5 years
  • Adenoma ≥10 mm, villous component or high grade dysplasia (advanced adenoma): 3 years
  • Piecemeal removal of a large polyp: early check at about 6 months
  • Hyperplastic polyp in the rectosigmoid: back to routine 10 year screening
exam_pearl: Size flips the interval: a small (<10 mm) single tubular adenoma earns a long interval, while ≥10 mm or villous histology earns 3 years.

stem: 43 male have family history of colon cancer underwent sigmoidoscopy for polyp removal. Histopathology showed tubular adenoma 1,3 cm completely removed... how to follow?

A. 3 to 6 months: an early repeat is only needed when a large polyp was removed piecemeal or incompletely; this one was completely removed.
C. 5 years: this fits a lower risk finding (for example 3 to 4 small tubular adenomas, or a first degree relative screening interval), not an adenoma ≥10 mm.
D. No need: an adenoma is premalignant and recurs in other sites, so surveillance is always required; "no further surveillance" applies only to a small rectosigmoid hyperplastic polyp (back to routine screening).

stem: 52 year old male medically free came to the clinic complaining of red urine for 2 days associated with right flank pain, no dysuria no fever no other symptoms. On examination: right flank tenderness and palpable rectal prostate (written like this). Urine culture: negative. Urine analysis: + erythrocyte, Nitrate: absent, WBC: absent. What is the most appropriate next investigation:
why_right: Red urine with right flank pain and loin tenderness, with no dysuria, no fever, negative culture and no pyuria or nitrites, points to a ureteric or renal stone rather than infection. The first line imaging for suspected urolithiasis is a non contrast CT KUB, which detects almost all stones and also shows other renal causes of hematuria.
why_wrong_block:
A. Urine cytology: an adjunct when urothelial cancer is suspected (painless gross hematuria in an older smoker); it has low sensitivity and is not the first test for painful hematuria with flank pain.
C. Retrograde urethrogram: used after pelvic trauma with blood at the meatus or suspected urethral injury, before passing a catheter; there is no trauma here.
D. Cystoscopy: evaluates the bladder in painless gross hematuria or when bladder pathology is suspected; flank pain directs the first test to the upper tract with CT.
key_concept:
Hematuria: let the pain and the context pick the first test.
  • Painful hematuria + flank/loin pain, no infection: non contrast CT KUB (stone)
  • Fever, dysuria, pyuria/nitrites: urinalysis and culture (UTI/pyelonephritis)
  • Painless gross hematuria, older, smoker: CT urography + cystoscopy (urothelial cancer)
  • Pelvic trauma + blood at meatus: retrograde urethrogram
  • Pregnancy or child with suspected stone: ultrasound first
exam_pearl: Remove the flank pain and make it painless hematuria in a smoker, and the answer becomes cystoscopy with CT urography.

stem: 12-year-old patient presents with a 4-hour history of right sided lower abdominal pain. Examination confirms a slightly elevated, tender right testis. The lie of the testis is horizontal with no redness or edema of the scrotum. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: lie of the testis is horizontal
why_right: An adolescent with acute pain of only 4 hours, a slightly elevated (high riding), tender testis with a horizontal lie is testicular torsion until proven otherwise. Torsion is a clinical diagnosis and a surgical emergency, so the most appropriate management is immediate scrotal exploration (detorsion and bilateral fixation, or orchidectomy if non viable) without waiting for imaging.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oral analgesics: pain relief alone wastes the salvage window while the testis infarcts; analgesia (NSAID) is the treatment for torsion of a testicular appendage with a blue dot sign and normal lie.
B. Oral antibiotics: treat epididymo-orchitis, which is more gradual with fever, dysuria and scrotal redness and swelling; this scrotum has no redness or edema.
C. Doppler ultrasound: only when the diagnosis is genuinely uncertain; with classic signs, imaging delays surgery and lowers testicular salvage.
key_concept:
Acute scrotum: decide by onset, lie and redness.
  • Torsion: sudden severe pain, high riding horizontal testis, absent cremasteric reflex: explore immediately
  • Torsion of appendage: upper pole tenderness, blue dot sign, normal vertical lie: NSAID, conservative
  • Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, fever/dysuria, red swollen scrotum, Doppler increased flow: antibiotics
  • Idiopathic scrotal edema: painless bilateral redness extending to the groins
  • Salvage is best within about 6 hours of onset
exam_pearl: Torsion can present as lower abdominal pain in a boy; always examine the scrotum, and do not let a Doppler delay the theatre.

stem: Severe left lower leg pain for 6 hours. When examined there's no pulse. What's source of thrombus?
why_right: Severe leg pain for 6 hours with no pulse is acute limb ischemia, and an acute occlusion like this is classically embolic. Most peripheral emboli are cardiac in origin, and the commonest single source is a thrombus in the left atrium (especially the left atrial appendage) due to atrial fibrillation, so the left atrium is the expected source when no other history is given.
why_wrong_block:
B. Left ventricle: a mural thrombus forms after a recent MI or with a ventricular aneurysm or dilated cardiomyopathy; it becomes the answer only when the stem mentions a recent MI.
C. Thoracic aorta: atheromatous plaque or aneurysm can shed emboli, but this is a much less common source than the heart.
D. Abdominal aorta: an aneurysm's mural thrombus can embolize distally (often small emboli to the toes), but it is an uncommon source compared with a cardiac thrombus.
key_concept:
Acute limb ischemia: embolus vs thrombosis.
  • Embolus: sudden onset, no prior claudication, often AF or recent MI, normal contralateral pulses
  • Embolic source: heart first (left atrium in AF most common; left ventricle after MI)
  • Thrombosis: on known atherosclerosis, prior claudication, more gradual onset
  • Same cardiac embolic sources cause acute mesenteric ischemia
  • 6 P's: pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia
exam_pearl: Add "MI 2 weeks ago" to the stem and the source becomes the left ventricular mural thrombus.

stem: Patient just got in MVA. He responded to 500ml saline. Complains of lower abdominal pain (pelvic region). No external bleeding. FAST is positive for free fluid in abdomen. Now he is stable. What's the best INITIAL investigation now?
why_right: A blunt trauma patient with pelvic (lower abdominal) pain who was hypotensive and responded to fluids is suspected of a pelvic fracture, a major source of hidden bleeding. The initial investigation is a plain pelvic x-ray, taken at the bedside as an adjunct to the primary survey, because it quickly shows an unstable pelvic ring that needs binding and changes the bleeding plan. Once stable, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis follows as the definitive study.
why_wrong_block:
A. This option was not remembered as a real choice in the recall (the original A and B were judged irrelevant), so it cannot be the answer.
D. Retrograde urethrogram: indicated when there are signs of urethral injury (blood at the meatus, high riding prostate, inability to void, scrotal or perineal hematoma) and before any Foley catheter; none of these signs are described.
key_concept:
Blunt abdominal and pelvic trauma, by stability.
  • Primary survey adjuncts: chest x-ray, pelvic x-ray, FAST
  • Stable (including transient responder now stable) + positive FAST: CT abdomen/pelvis
  • Unstable + positive FAST: laparotomy
  • Unstable + negative FAST: DPL, and think pelvic or retroperitoneal bleeding
  • Blood at meatus after pelvic fracture: retrograde urethrogram first, then suprapubic catheter (no Foley)
exam_pearl: "Initial" with pelvic pain means the bedside pelvic x-ray; if CT were offered and the question asked for the most definitive test in a now stable patient, CT would win.

stem: A man presented with trauma to his chest complains of severe pain in his chest, he has severe tenderness on the chest with multiple bruises. During initial assessment the airways are patent and clear, he is alert and conscious but his chest wall is unstable when he moves or tries to take a deep breath and bruising in his right chest. Air sounds present bilaterally clear. Vital signs normal apart from saturation 86%. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A chest wall that is unstable when he breathes, with multiple bruises and severe tenderness, describes a flail chest (multiple rib fractures with paradoxical movement). The airway is patent, he is alert, breath sounds are clear bilaterally and vitals are otherwise normal, so treatment is supportive: oxygen and adequate IV analgesia, which lets him breathe deeply and cough and often corrects the hypoxemia caused by splinting and the underlying lung contusion.
why_wrong_block:
B. Mechanical ventilation: reserved for flail chest with respiratory failure that persists despite oxygen and good analgesia, exhaustion or a falling conscious level; this patient is alert and protecting his airway.
C. Chest tube: for a pneumothorax or hemothorax; breath sounds are present and clear on both sides, so there is no pleural collection to drain.
D. Emergency thoracotomy: for massive hemothorax (about 1500 mL on insertion or 200 to 300 mL per hour), traumatic arrest or decompensation after stabilization; none applies.
key_concept:
Flail chest: treat the pain and the contused lung, not the ribs.
  • Definition: multiple adjacent ribs broken in more than one place, paradoxical movement
  • First line: oxygen + strong analgesia (IV opioids, regional or epidural block) + chest physiotherapy
  • Ventilate only if respiratory failure persists or the patient tires
  • Avoid fluid overload because of the underlying pulmonary contusion
  • Chest tube only if pneumothorax/hemothorax; thoracotomy only for massive bleeding
exam_pearl: Add drowsiness, exhaustion or worsening hypoxia despite analgesia and oxygen, and the answer becomes intubation and ventilation.

stem: Pt came after road traffic accident, was stable but suddenly desaturated spo2 ~88%. Chest X ray was NORMAL. What you will do next?
key_concept:
Sudden desaturation after blunt trauma with a normal first chest x-ray: think of lesions that evolve or hide.
  • Pulmonary contusion: x-ray changes can lag hours after injury
  • Pneumothorax: may be occult on a supine film or develop later
  • Fat embolism: long bone fractures, typically 24 to 72 hours later, with confusion and petechiae
  • Pulmonary embolism: immobilized trauma patient, later in the course
  • Always: oxygen and ABCDE reassessment first; ABG confirms hypoxemia and gas exchange
exam_pearl: Watch the lead-in: "next investigation for gas exchange" favors ABG, while "repeat after an interval" wording points to an evolving contusion or pneumothorax.

stem: 24-year-old male presents with RLQ pain and fever, diagnosed with acute appendicitis and was taken to OR for appendectomy using a Gridiron (McBurney's) incision. During surgery, the surgeon found a normal appendix. What is the appropriate action?
OptB: Resect the appendix and close the abdomen
why_right: A normal appendix found at operation for presumed appendicitis means the real cause of the RLQ pain and fever is still in the abdomen. The surgeon must not simply close: the standard move is to search for an alternative pathology through the same incision, and in a young male the classic one to exclude is an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum, found by running the terminal ileum (about 2 feet / 60 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve). Other things checked are mesenteric nodes (mesenteric adenitis), the terminal ileum (Crohn's) and, in females, the adnexa.
why_wrong_block:
A. Closing without exploring leaves the true source of fever and RLQ pain (e.g., Meckel's diverticulitis, ileitis) untreated and missed.
B. Removing the normal appendix is commonly done as well, but only after the abdomen has been examined for another cause; removing it and closing at once skips the key step this question tests.
D. Conversion to a midline laparotomy is reserved for pathology that cannot be reached or managed through the gridiron incision (e.g., generalized peritonitis, perforated viscus elsewhere); it is not the first move for a normal appendix.
key_concept:
Normal appendix at appendectomy: explore for another cause before closing.
  • Run the terminal ileum: Meckel's diverticulitis, Crohn's ileitis
  • Look at mesentery: mesenteric adenitis
  • Females: check ovaries and tubes (ruptured cyst, torsion, PID, ectopic)
  • Normal appendix is usually removed too, to avoid future diagnostic confusion
  • Extend or convert the incision only if the found pathology demands it
exam_pearl: Meckel's rule of 2s: about 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, so run the terminal ileum before closing on a normal appendix.

stem: 10 or 12 y child on bicycle was hit by a car, what is the best confirmation to consciousness?
OptD: Signs of truma on the head
why_right: After head trauma (child hit by a car on a bicycle), the standardized, reproducible measure of level of consciousness is the Glasgow Coma Scale. It combines eye opening (1 to 4), verbal response (1 to 5) and motor response (1 to 6) into a total of 3 to 15, and serial scores track deterioration. A pediatric verbal scale is used in young children, but at 10 to 12 years the standard GCS applies.
why_wrong_block:
B. Orientation to time, place and person is only one item of the GCS (verbal 5); on its own it does not grade eye or motor response and cannot quantify a depressed level.
C. Being able to describe the accident tests memory (absence of amnesia), not a graded level of consciousness; useful in concussion history but not the confirmation tool.
D. Visible head trauma shows mechanism and injury, not the patient's level of consciousness; serious brain injury can occur with no external signs.
key_concept:
Level of consciousness in trauma = GCS (E4 V5 M6, range 3 to 15).
  • Eye: 4 spontaneous, 3 to speech, 2 to pain, 1 none
  • Verbal: 5 oriented, 4 confused, 3 inappropriate words, 2 sounds, 1 none
  • Motor: 6 obeys, 5 localizes, 4 withdraws, 3 abnormal flexion, 2 extension, 1 none
  • GCS ≤ 8: secure the airway (intubate)
  • Quick primary-survey alternative: AVPU
exam_pearl: Orientation is a GCS component, not a substitute for it; the question asks for the whole graded tool.

stem: 68-year-old man presented complaining of abdominal pain, vomiting, and jaundice. Labs: liver profile all high & CA19-9 very high. What is your diagnosis? Options included: . CA19:510
key_concept:
Older patient + obstructive jaundice + very high CA19-9: think pancreatic head (periampullary) cancer.
  • CA19-9: pancreatic/biliary marker; AFP: hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Distended gallbladder + dilated intra and extrahepatic ducts: distal (pancreatic head) obstruction
  • Shrunken gallbladder + intrahepatic dilation only: hilar (Klatskin) tumor
  • Imaging: double duct sign on CT
  • The fuller versions of this recall are keyed to carcinoma of the head of the pancreas
exam_pearl: CA19-9 points to the pancreas or bile ducts; AFP points to the liver.

stem: Patient with jaundice, dark urine, pale stool and weight loss. found to have hugely distended gall bladder. High bilirubin. Elevated liver enzymes. GGT 213. Ca 19- 9 502. What is the cause?
OptB: Carcinoma of the head of the pancrease
highlight_terms_source: jaundice, dark urine, pale stool and weight loss
why_right: Painless-type obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stool) with weight loss, a hugely distended gallbladder (Courvoisier sign) and a very high CA19-9 indicates a malignant obstruction distal to the cystic duct. The classic cause is carcinoma of the head of the pancreas, which compresses the distal CBD so bile backs up and distends the gallbladder.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mirizzi syndrome is extrinsic compression of the common hepatic duct by a stone impacted in the cystic duct or Hartmann pouch; it presents with RUQ pain and cholecystitis features and a stone-filled, usually contracted gallbladder, not weight loss with a huge gallbladder and high CA19-9.
C. Distal CBD obstruction describes the level of the block, not its cause; the question asks for the cause, and weight loss with CA19-9 identifies it as pancreatic head cancer. A distal CBD stone would also give painful, fluctuating jaundice with a non-palpable gallbladder.
key_concept:
Courvoisier law: jaundice + palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be stones; think malignancy.
  • Pancreatic head/periampullary: distended gallbladder, dilated intra and extrahepatic ducts
  • Klatskin: shrunken gallbladder, intrahepatic dilation only
  • Stones: fibrosed non-palpable gallbladder, painful fluctuating jaundice
  • Clues to malignancy: weight loss, anorexia, high CA19-9
exam_pearl: 'Distal CBD obstruction' is a level, not a cause; when CA19-9 and weight loss are given, name the tumor.

stem: 68-year-old Male patient was complaining of yellowish discoloration, epigastric pain, dark urine, pale stool and weight loss. On examination the patient was jaundiced and on palpation tenderness in the epigastric region and right upper quadrant. The gallbladder was palpable and tender. Labs showed: Elevated liver enzymes, high total and direct bilirubin, high ALP, GGT 213, CA19-9: 502. Ultrasound showed hugely dilated common bile duct and gallbladder. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
OptD: Cancer of the head of the pancreas
highlight_terms_source: dark urine, pale stool and weight loss
hugely dilated common bile duct and gallbladder
why_right: A 68-year-old with weight loss, obstructive jaundice (dark urine, pale stool, high direct bilirubin, ALP, GGT), a palpable gallbladder, hugely dilated CBD and gallbladder on ultrasound and CA19-9 502 has malignant distal biliary obstruction. The most likely cause is cancer of the head of the pancreas, which blocks the distal CBD and distends the gallbladder (Courvoisier sign).
why_wrong_block:
A. Mirizzi syndrome obstructs the common hepatic duct from a stone in the cystic duct/Hartmann pouch, so the CBD below it is not dilated and the gallbladder is usually stone-filled and contracted; it does not explain weight loss or CA19-9 of 502.
B. Liver metastases cause hepatomegaly and intrahepatic or hilar obstruction at most; they do not produce a hugely dilated CBD with a distended gallbladder.
C. Distal CBD obstruction is the anatomical level shown on ultrasound, not the underlying cause; the question asks for the cause, and age, weight loss and CA19-9 point to a pancreatic head tumor.
key_concept:
Where the duct dilation stops tells you where the block is.
  • Dilated CBD + distended gallbladder: distal block (pancreatic head, ampulla, distal CBD)
  • Intrahepatic dilation only + collapsed gallbladder: hilar Klatskin tumor
  • Dilated CHD with normal CBD + cystic duct stone: Mirizzi
  • Malignancy clues: age, weight loss, high CA19-9
  • Next imaging: contrast CT (double duct sign)
exam_pearl: Courvoisier classically describes a non-tender gallbladder; a tender one here does not overturn the weight loss, huge CBD and CA19-9.

stem: Young male (around 20) Pt presented after he has a blunt abdominal trauma CT : there was Extravasation around the left kidney What are most appropriate step in management ?
key_concept:
Blunt renal trauma: stability decides, then the type of extravasation.
  • Unstable despite resuscitation: surgical exploration (repair or nephrectomy)
  • Stable + active arterial blush: angioembolization
  • Stable, no active bleeding: non-operative (fluids, observe, serial Hb)
  • Urinary extravasation: mostly observe; ureteric stent if persistent
  • Stable abdominal trauma is imaged with contrast CT
exam_pearl: 'Extravasation' alone does not mean surgery: ask whether it is blood (blush, embolize if stable) or urine (usually observe).

stem: Female pt presented with axillary mass 3x3 on examination the mass was soft and movable Next appropriate step in management
key_concept:
Axillary mass in a woman: image first, biopsy if suspicious, reassure only when clearly benign.
  • Over 30: mammogram ± ultrasound; under 30: ultrasound
  • Suspicious node or solid lesion: core needle biopsy
  • Soft, mobile, rubbery: lipoma or accessory breast tissue likely
  • Hard, fixed, matted: malignancy (breast primary, lymphoma) until proven otherwise
exam_pearl: Soft and mobile lowers suspicion, but a new axillary mass still gets imaging before reassurance.

stem: 32 yo Pregnant women G3P2 at 28 weeks came to the clinic complaining of right breast mass which first noticed 4 months ago, on examination you find round, soft and mobile, movable, right breast mass. No skin change What most appropriate next step or (management?)?
why_right: A breast mass in a pregnant woman (28 weeks) present for 4 months must be evaluated now, and the first and safest imaging in pregnancy is ultrasound. It distinguishes cystic from solid lesions without radiation, and bilateral scanning assesses both breasts and the axillae. A suspicious solid lesion then goes on to core biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Mammography is the first choice in a non-pregnant woman over 30; in pregnancy it is not absolutely contraindicated but is less sensitive in dense breasts and needs radiation, so ultrasound comes first.
C. FNA (or core biopsy) follows imaging, not before it; ultrasound first decides whether the mass is a cyst (aspirate) or solid (core biopsy).
D. Deferring until after delivery risks missing pregnancy-associated breast cancer; soft and mobile features are reassuring but a 4-month mass in pregnancy still needs imaging now.
key_concept:
Breast mass in pregnancy: ultrasound first, never wait for delivery.
  • Pregnant or under 30: ultrasound
  • Non-pregnant over 30: diagnostic mammogram ± ultrasound
  • Solid on imaging: core needle biopsy
  • Cystic: FNA
exam_pearl: Benign-feeling mass in pregnancy is still imaged now; 'reassess after delivery' is the trap.

stem: A 32-year-old woman a 28-week pregnant presents with an enlarging right breast mass that has been present for 4 months and is associated with mild pain. Physical examination confirmed a 3 x 2 cm firm movable mass not associated with skin changes or enlarged axillary lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: An enlarging breast mass in a 28-week pregnant woman needs workup now, and the lead-in asks for the next step. Ultrasound is the safest first imaging in pregnancy: no radiation and better than mammography in the dense pregnant breast. Bilateral ultrasound characterizes the 3 x 2 cm mass and checks the other breast and axillae before any biopsy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Fine needle aspiration comes after imaging; ultrasound first decides between cyst (aspirate) and solid lesion (core biopsy).
C. Diagnostic mammography would be first in a non-pregnant woman over 30; in pregnancy it is not absolutely contraindicated but ultrasound is done first.
D. An enlarging mass in pregnancy must not be deferred; delay risks missing pregnancy-associated breast cancer.
key_concept:
Breast mass in pregnancy: ultrasound is the first imaging.
  • Pregnant or under 30: ultrasound
  • Non-pregnant over 30: diagnostic mammogram ± ultrasound
  • Solid or suspicious on ultrasound: core needle biopsy
  • Simple cyst: aspiration
exam_pearl: Pregnancy flips the first imaging from mammogram to ultrasound; it never justifies waiting until delivery.

stem: 23 year old presented with abdominal distention and tenderness was diagnosed with bowel obstruction He hax no medical or surgical history What is the cause of the distention ?
why_right: Adhesions are the most common cause of small bowel obstruction overall, but they need prior abdominal surgery (or peritoneal inflammation). This 23-year-old has no surgical history (a 'virgin abdomen'), so the most likely cause of his obstruction is a hernia, the commonest cause after adhesions and the leading cause when there has been no previous surgery. Examine the groin and umbilicus for an incarcerated hernia.
why_wrong_block:
B. Adhesions are the top cause of SBO only when there is a history of abdominal surgery (or inflammation such as abdominal TB); here there is none.
C. Meckel's diverticulum can cause obstruction (volvulus, intussusception) in young patients but is much less common than a hernia; it is more typical in children, and often with painless rectal bleeding.
D. This option was not recalled by the source and was described as irrelevant.
key_concept:
Cause of SBO depends on surgical history.
  • Previous abdominal surgery: adhesions
  • No previous surgery (virgin abdomen): hernia (check groin, umbilicus)
  • Large bowel obstruction in older adults: colorectal cancer, then volvulus, diverticular stricture
  • Other SBO causes: Crohn stricture, Meckel's, gallstone ileus, intussusception with a lead point
exam_pearl: 'No surgical history' is the clue that removes adhesions and makes hernia the answer.
